levels.title: What is Perimeter?
levels.mia: Hi! I'm Mia 🦊 Today we start a brand-new chapter: Mensuration! Let's begin with perimeter.
levels.body:
Mensuration is the branch of maths that deals with measurement of shapes — how long their boundary is, and how much surface they cover.

The perimeter of a closed shape is the total length of its boundary — the distance you would walk if you walked all the way around the outside of the shape once.

Example: A rectangular park is 6 cm long and 3 cm wide on a map. Walking all the way around it means walking 6 + 3 + 6 + 3 = 18 cm on the map.

check.q: Tap to think: if a shape has sides 4 cm, 5 cm, and 6 cm, what do you add to find its perimeter?
check.answer: You add all three sides: 4 + 5 + 6 = 15 cm. That is the perimeter.

levels.miaWin: Great start! You already understand what perimeter means! 🎉

levels.title: Measuring the Boundary
levels.mia: Perimeter always has a unit of length — like cm, m, or km — because it is a length, not a space.
levels.body:
To find the perimeter of ANY closed shape (however many sides it has), the rule is always the same: add up the lengths of all the sides.

For shapes with straight sides, you can measure each side with a ruler and add them. For curved shapes (like a circle), a thread can be wrapped around the boundary and then measured with a ruler.

Example: A triangular garden has sides 5 cm, 4 cm, and 3 cm on a plan. Perimeter = 5 + 4 + 3 = 12 cm.
💡 Tip: Perimeter is always measured in units of length (cm, m, km) — never in square units.

check.q: Tap to check: what tool can you use to find the perimeter of a curved shape like a circle?
check.answer: Wrap a thread around the boundary, mark where it meets, then measure the thread's length with a ruler — that gives the perimeter.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You know how to measure boundaries of any shape now! ⭐

levels.title: Perimeter in Everyday Life
levels.mia: Perimeter is not just a maths idea — people use it every day to plan real things!
levels.body:
Perimeter helps us figure out how much material is needed to go AROUND something — like fencing a field, framing a photo, or putting lace around a tablecloth.

Example: A farmer wants to fence a rectangular field that is 50 m long and 30 m wide. He needs wire equal to the perimeter: 2 × (50 + 30) = 160 m of wire.
💡 Tip: Whenever a problem talks about fencing, boundary wire, border, or edging — it is asking about perimeter!

check.q: Tap to think: would putting a ribbon border around a square photo frame need the perimeter or the area of the frame?
check.answer: The perimeter — a border/ribbon goes around the boundary, which is exactly what perimeter measures.

levels.miaWin: Excellent! You can now spot perimeter problems in real life! 🚀

levels.title: What Makes a Shape 'Regular'?
levels.mia: A regular shape is extra neat — all its sides AND all its angles are equal!
levels.body:
A regular polygon is a closed shape where every side has the same length and every angle has the same measure. An equilateral triangle, a square, a regular pentagon, and a regular hexagon are all regular polygons.

Example: A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides. If one side is 4 cm, every other side is also 4 cm.

check.q: Tap to check: is a rectangle (non-square) a regular polygon?
check.answer: No — a rectangle has equal opposite sides but not all four sides equal, so it is not a regular polygon.

levels.miaWin: You have got it! Regular shapes are all about equal sides! 🎉

levels.title: The Shortcut Formula
levels.mia: Since all sides of a regular polygon are equal, there is a quick shortcut to find its perimeter!
levels.body:
Instead of adding the same length again and again, you can simply multiply:

💡 Perimeter of a regular polygon = Number of sides × Length of one side
Example: A regular pentagon (5 sides) has each side 7 cm. Perimeter = 5 × 7 = 35 cm.

check.q: Tap to think: a regular octagon (8 sides) has each side 3 cm. What is its perimeter?
check.answer: Perimeter = 8 × 3 = 24 cm.

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You just used multiplication to save time! ⭐

levels.title: Comparing Regular Shapes
levels.mia: Let's compare a few regular shapes to see how the formula works for each one.
levels.body:
Here is the shortcut applied to the most common regular shapes you will meet:

• Equilateral triangle (3 sides): Perimeter = 3 × side
• Square (4 sides): Perimeter = 4 × side
• Regular pentagon (5 sides): Perimeter = 5 × side
• Regular hexagon (6 sides): Perimeter = 6 × side

Example: Even though both shapes above have a side of 6 cm, the hexagon has a bigger perimeter because it has more sides.

check.q: Tap to check: which has a bigger perimeter — a square of side 5 cm, or a regular pentagon of side 5 cm?
check.answer: The regular pentagon (5 × 5 = 25 cm) has a bigger perimeter than the square (4 × 5 = 20 cm), since it has more sides.

levels.miaWin: Superb! You can now compare regular shapes with confidence! 🚀

levels.title: Sides of a Rectangle
levels.mia: A rectangle has 2 pairs of equal sides — that gives us a neat shortcut for its perimeter!
levels.body:
A rectangle has a length and a breadth (also called width). Opposite sides of a rectangle are always equal, so a rectangle has two long sides (length) and two short sides (breadth).

Example: A rectangular notebook cover has length 8 cm and breadth 4 cm on a diagram — that means BOTH long sides are 8 cm and BOTH short sides are 4 cm.

check.q: Tap to think: if one long side of a rectangle is 10 cm, what is the other long side?
check.answer: Also 10 cm — opposite sides of a rectangle are always equal.

levels.miaWin: Nice! You know the key property of a rectangle now! 🎉

levels.title: The Rectangle Perimeter Formula
levels.mia: Let's turn 'length + breadth + length + breadth' into a short formula!
levels.body:
Perimeter = length + breadth + length + breadth = 2 × length + 2 × breadth

💡 Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 × (length + breadth)
Example: Length = 9 cm, breadth = 5 cm. Perimeter = 2 × (9 + 5) = 2 × 14 = 28 cm.

check.q: Tap to check: a rectangle has length 12 cm and breadth 7 cm. What is its perimeter?

levels.miaWin: You have mastered the rectangle formula! ⭐

levels.title: Working Backwards
levels.mia: Sometimes you know the perimeter and one side — and need to find the missing side!
levels.body:
If you know the perimeter and the length, you can find the breadth by reversing the formula step by step.

Perimeter = 2 × (length + breadth), so: length + breadth = Perimeter ÷ 2, and then breadth = (Perimeter ÷ 2) − length.

Example: A rectangular table has perimeter 30 cm (on a plan) and length 9 cm. Half the perimeter is 15 cm, so breadth = 15 − 9 = 6 cm.
💡 Tip: Always find half the perimeter first — that equals length + breadth together.

check.q: Tap to try: a rectangle has perimeter 40 cm and breadth 8 cm. What is its length?
check.answer: Half of 40 is 20, so length + breadth = 20. Length = 20 − 8 = 12 cm.

levels.miaWin: Amazing! You can now solve for a missing side too! 🚀

levels.title: Every Side is the Same
levels.mia: A square is the friendliest shape for perimeter — all 4 sides are exactly equal!
levels.body:
A square has 4 sides, and all 4 are equal in length. Because of this, we do not need to add four different numbers — we can just multiply one side by 4.

Example: A square tile has each side 5 cm. All four sides are 5 cm, 5 cm, 5 cm, and 5 cm.

check.q: Tap to think: if one side of a square is 9 cm, what are the other three sides?
check.answer: All the other three sides are also 9 cm each — a square always has 4 equal sides.

levels.miaWin: Great! You know why squares are special now! 🎉

levels.title: The Square Perimeter Formula
levels.mia: Adding the same number four times is the same as multiplying by 4!
levels.body:
💡 Perimeter of a square = 4 × side

This is simply side + side + side + side written as a quick multiplication.

Example: A square garden has side 6 m. Perimeter = 4 × 6 = 24 m of fencing needed.

check.q: Tap to check: a square has side 15 cm. What is its perimeter?
check.answer: Perimeter = 4 × 15 = 60 cm.

levels.miaWin: You have got the square formula down perfectly! ⭐

levels.title: Finding the Side from the Perimeter
levels.mia: What if you are given the perimeter and asked to find the side instead?
levels.body:
Since Perimeter = 4 × side, we can reverse it: side = Perimeter ÷ 4.

Example: A square plot has a perimeter of 48 m. Side = 48 ÷ 4 = 12 m.
💡 Tip: This trick only works for squares, because all 4 sides are equal — for a rectangle you need both length and breadth information.

check.q: Tap to try: a square has a perimeter of 100 cm. What is the length of one side?

levels.miaWin: Excellent work reversing the formula! 🚀

levels.title: Three Sides to Add
levels.mia: A triangle has only 3 sides — and unlike a square, they can all be different lengths!
levels.body:
Triangles can be of different types based on their sides: a scalene triangle has all sides different, an isosceles triangle has two sides equal, and an equilateral triangle has all three sides equal.

Example: A scalene triangle has sides 7 cm, 8 cm, and 9 cm — all different lengths, so we must add all three separately.

check.q: Tap to think: what is special about the sides of an equilateral triangle?
check.answer: All three sides of an equilateral triangle are equal in length.

levels.miaWin: Great! You now know the different types of triangles! 🎉

levels.title: The General Triangle Formula
levels.mia: No matter what type of triangle it is, the rule for perimeter never changes.
levels.body:
💡 Perimeter of a triangle = side 1 + side 2 + side 3

For an equilateral triangle, since all sides are equal, this becomes a shortcut: Perimeter = 3 × side.

Example: An equilateral triangle has each side 6 cm. Perimeter = 3 × 6 = 18 cm.

check.q: Tap to check: an isosceles triangle has two sides of 5 cm each and a third side of 7 cm. What is its perimeter?
check.answer: Perimeter = 5 + 5 + 7 = 17 cm.

levels.miaWin: You can now find the perimeter of any triangle! ⭐

levels.title: Missing Side of a Triangle
levels.mia: Sometimes you know the perimeter and two sides, and need to find the third!
levels.body:
If you know the perimeter and two sides, subtract both known sides from the perimeter to get the third side.

Example: A triangle has perimeter 20 cm, with two sides 6 cm and 7 cm. Third side = 20 − (6 + 7) = 20 − 13 = 7 cm.
💡 Tip: Always add the two known sides first, then subtract that total from the perimeter.

check.q: Tap to try: a triangle has perimeter 24 cm, with two sides 9 cm and 8 cm. What is the third side?

levels.miaWin: Wonderful! You can solve for any missing triangle side now! 🚀

levels.title: What is Area?
levels.mia: Perimeter measures the boundary — but area measures something completely different: the surface INSIDE the shape!
levels.body:
The area of a closed shape is the amount of flat surface it covers. Think of area as how much paint you would need to colour the entire inside of a shape.

Example: A rectangle made up of 18 small identical squares has an area of 18 square units — we simply count the squares that fit inside.

check.q: Tap to think: does area measure the boundary of a shape or the surface inside it?
check.answer: Area measures the surface inside the shape, not the boundary. (The boundary length is the perimeter.)

levels.miaWin: Great! You now understand what area really means! 🎉

levels.title: Measuring Area with Unit Squares
levels.mia: To measure area, we count how many little unit squares fit exactly inside a shape.
levels.body:
Area is measured in square units — like square centimetres (cm²), square metres (m²), because we are measuring a flat surface, made up of tiny unit squares.

Example: A rectangle covers a grid that is 5 squares wide and 4 squares tall. Counting all the squares: 5 × 4 = 20 squares, so the area is 20 cm².
💡 Tip: Area is always written with a small '2' after the unit — like cm² or m² — never just cm or m.

check.q: Tap to check: which unit is correct for area — 12 cm or 12 cm²?
check.answer: 12 cm² is correct for area, since area is always measured in square units.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You know how to measure area with unit squares now! ⭐

levels.title: Perimeter vs Area — Do Not Mix Them Up!
levels.mia: Perimeter and area are easy to confuse — let's make the difference crystal clear.
levels.body:
Perimeter is a length around a shape (measured in cm, m). Area is the surface inside a shape (measured in cm², m²). Two shapes can have the same perimeter but different areas, or the same area but different perimeters!

Example: Walking around a garden measures its perimeter. Covering the whole garden with grass measures its area.

check.q: Tap to think: if you want to know how much carpet is needed to cover a floor, do you need perimeter or area?
check.answer: Area — covering a surface (like a floor with carpet) always needs area, not perimeter.

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You can now tell perimeter and area apart every time! 🚀

levels.title: Counting Rows and Columns
levels.mia: Instead of counting every single square one by one, there is a much faster way for rectangles!
levels.body:
Imagine a rectangle divided into a grid of unit squares. If it has 6 columns and 4 rows of squares, you could count all 24 squares one by one — or you could simply multiply 6 × 4!

Example: A rectangle has 6 squares across and 4 squares down. Total squares = 6 × 4 = 24 unit squares.

check.q: Tap to think: a grid has 7 columns and 3 rows of unit squares. How many squares in total?
check.answer: 7 × 3 = 21 unit squares.

levels.miaWin: Great! You have discovered the multiplication shortcut! 🎉

levels.title: The Rectangle Area Formula
levels.mia: That shortcut has a name — length times breadth!
levels.body:
💡 Area of a rectangle = length × breadth

The number of squares across equals the length, and the number of squares down equals the breadth — so multiplying them gives the total area directly.

Example: A rectangular table top has length 8 cm and breadth 3 cm. Area = 8 × 3 = 24 cm².

check.q: Tap to check: a rectangular field has length 40 m and breadth 25 m. What is its area?

levels.miaWin: You have mastered the rectangle area formula! ⭐

levels.title: Finding a Missing Side from Area
levels.mia: If you know the area and one side, you can always find the other side!
levels.body:
Since Area = length × breadth, if you know the area and the length, then: breadth = Area ÷ length.

Example: A rectangular wall has area 48 m² and length 8 m. Breadth = 48 ÷ 8 = 6 m.
💡 Tip: Whenever area is given with one side, use division — the opposite of multiplication — to find the missing side.

check.q: Tap to try: a rectangle has area 60 cm² and breadth 5 cm. What is its length?
check.answer: Length = 60 ÷ 5 = 12 cm.

levels.miaWin: Superb! You can now find any missing side using area! 🚀

levels.title: A Rectangle with Equal Sides
levels.mia: A square is just a special rectangle where length and breadth are the same — so the area rule still works!
levels.body:
Since a square has length = breadth = side, the rectangle formula (length × breadth) becomes side × side.

Example: A square has 4 unit squares across and 4 down. Area = 4 × 4 = 16 unit squares.

check.q: Tap to think: why does the rectangle formula length × breadth also work for a square?
check.answer: Because in a square, length and breadth are equal (both are called the 'side'), so length × breadth becomes side × side.

levels.miaWin: Great connection! You see how squares and rectangles relate! 🎉

levels.title: The Square Area Formula
levels.mia: Side × side is also called squaring a number — that is where squares get their name!
levels.body:
💡 Area of a square = side × side = side²
Example: A square tile has side 5 cm. Area = 5 × 5 = 25 cm².
💡 Tip: 'side²' means side × side, not side × 2 — do not confuse squaring with doubling!

check.q: Tap to check: a square has side 9 cm. What is its area?
check.answer: Area = 9 × 9 = 81 cm².

levels.miaWin: You have mastered the square area formula! ⭐

levels.title: Finding the Side from the Area
levels.mia: What if you know the area and need to find the side length?
levels.body:
Since Area = side × side, you need to find a number that, when multiplied by itself, gives the area. This is called finding the square root.

Example: A square garden has area 49 m². Since 7 × 7 = 49, the side of the garden is 7 m.

check.q: Tap to try: a square has area 64 cm². What is the length of its side?
check.answer: Side = 8 cm, because 8 × 8 = 64.

levels.miaWin: Excellent! You can now work backwards from area to side! 🚀

levels.title: Shapes That Are Not Perfect Rectangles
levels.mia: Not every shape is a neat rectangle or square — leaves, footprints, and lakes have irregular outlines!
levels.body:
For irregular shapes, we estimate the area by placing the shape on a squared graph paper (grid) and counting the unit squares it covers.

Example: Tracing a leaf on graph paper, you might count 10 full squares and 6 half squares covered by the leaf's outline.

check.q: Tap to think: why do we use squared graph paper to find the area of an irregular shape?
check.answer: Because the small squares act as unit squares we can count, letting us estimate the area even when the shape's boundary is not straight.

levels.miaWin: Great! You now know how to handle tricky, irregular shapes! 🎉

levels.title: The Counting Rule
levels.mia: There is a simple, agreed rule for counting squares on graph paper for irregular shapes.
levels.body:
The standard counting rule used in Class 6 is:

• Count a square as 1 if it is more than half-covered (or fully covered)
• Ignore a square if it is less than half-covered
• Count a square as 1/2 if it is exactly half-covered

Example: If a shape covers 8 full squares and 4 half squares, area ≈ 8 + (4 × 1/2) = 8 + 2 = 10 square units.
💡 Tip: This method only gives an ESTIMATE of the area — not an exact value — because the shape's edges are curved or uneven.

check.q: Tap to check: a traced shape covers 6 full squares and 8 half squares. What is the estimated area?
check.answer: Area ≈ 6 + (8 × 1/2) = 6 + 4 = 10 square units.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You know the official counting rule now! ⭐

levels.title: Practising the Estimate
levels.mia: Let's put the counting rule to work on a few more examples.
levels.body:
Remember: full or more-than-half squares count as 1, half squares count as 1/2, and less-than-half squares are ignored (count as 0).

Example: A map of a small pond covers 12 full squares and 5 half squares on graph paper. Area ≈ 12 + (5 × 1/2) = 12 + 2.5 = 14.5 square units.

check.q: Tap to try: a shape covers 15 full squares and 10 half squares. What is its estimated area?
check.answer: Area ≈ 15 + (10 × 1/2) = 15 + 5 = 20 square units.

levels.miaWin: Wonderful! You can estimate the area of any irregular shape now! 🚀

levels.title: Choosing Perimeter or Area
levels.mia: The biggest real-life skill in Mensuration is knowing WHICH one to use — perimeter or area!
levels.body:
Use perimeter when a problem is about the boundary — fencing, wire, border, edging, or framing. Use area when a problem is about covering a surface — flooring, painting, tiling, or carpeting.

Example: Buying a garland to go around a room's edge needs perimeter. Buying paint for the walls needs area.

check.q: Tap to think: does laying a carpet on a floor need perimeter or area?
check.answer: Area — a carpet covers the entire surface of the floor, so we need the area.

levels.miaWin: Great! You now know how to pick the right tool for the job! 🎉

levels.title: Cost Problems Using Perimeter
levels.mia: Once you find the perimeter, you can also find the COST of fencing or bordering!
levels.body:
💡 Total cost = Perimeter × Cost per unit length
Example: A field 40 m by 20 m needs fencing at ₹15 per metre. Perimeter = 2 × (40+20) = 120 m. Cost = 120 × 15 = ₹1800.

check.q: Tap to check: a square garden of side 15 m needs fencing at ₹10 per metre. What is the total cost?
check.answer: Perimeter = 4 × 15 = 60 m. Cost = 60 × 10 = ₹600.

levels.miaWin: You can now solve real fencing-cost problems! ⭐

levels.title: Cost Problems Using Area
levels.mia: Just like perimeter, area also helps us find the cost of covering a surface!
levels.body:
💡 Total cost = Area × Cost per square unit
Example: A room floor 6 m by 4 m needs tiles costing ₹200 per square metre. Area = 6 × 4 = 24 m². Cost = 24 × 200 = ₹4800.
💡 Tip: Always check the unit of the rate — 'per metre' means use perimeter, 'per square metre' means use area.

check.q: Tap to try: a rectangular wall 5 m by 3 m is painted at ₹50 per square metre. What is the total cost?

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You can now solve real-world area-cost problems too! 🚀

levels.title: Reading the Problem Carefully
levels.mia: Word problems can look tricky, but breaking them into small steps always helps!
levels.body:
When solving a Mensuration word problem, follow these steps: (1) Read carefully and note down the given values, (2) decide if you need perimeter or area, (3) write the correct formula, (4) substitute values and calculate, (5) write the answer with the correct unit.

Example: "A rectangular plot is 25 m long and 15 m wide. Find the cost of fencing it at ₹20 per metre." Step 1: length=25, breadth=15, rate=20. Step 2: fencing means perimeter. Step 3: P = 2(l+b). Step 4: P = 2(40) = 80 m, cost = 80×20 = ₹1600.

check.q: Tap to think: what is the very first thing you should do when solving a word problem?
check.answer: Read the problem carefully and write down all the given values — this helps you choose the correct formula.

levels.miaWin: Great! You now have a clear method for word problems! 🎉

levels.title: Combining Perimeter and Area
levels.mia: Some word problems ask about BOTH perimeter and area in the same question!
levels.body:
Read each part of the question separately — one part might need perimeter, and another might need area, even within the same problem.

Example: "A hall is 12 m long and 8 m wide. Find (a) the length of a wire needed to go around it once, and (b) the area of carpet needed to cover the floor." (a) is perimeter = 2(12+8) = 40 m. (b) is area = 12×8 = 96 m².

check.q: Tap to check: a square field has side 20 m. What is BOTH its perimeter and its area?
check.answer: Perimeter = 4 × 20 = 80 m. Area = 20 × 20 = 400 m².

levels.miaWin: Excellent! You can now handle multi-part questions! ⭐

levels.title: Comparing Two Shapes
levels.mia: Some tricky word problems ask you to compare two different shapes!
levels.body:
To compare shapes, calculate the perimeter or area of EACH shape separately using its own formula, then compare the two results.

Example: "Which has a bigger perimeter: a square of side 10 m, or a rectangle 12 m by 6 m?" Square: 4×10=40 m. Rectangle: 2×(12+6)=36 m. The square has the bigger perimeter.
💡 Tip: Two shapes can have the SAME perimeter but DIFFERENT areas, or the same area but different perimeters — always calculate both separately, do not assume!

check.q: Tap to try: which has more area — a square of side 8 m, or a rectangle 10 m by 6 m?
check.answer: Square area = 8×8 = 64 m². Rectangle area = 10×6 = 60 m². The square has more area.

levels.miaWin: Superb! You can now confidently compare any two shapes! 🚀

levels.title: Quick Recall — Key Facts
levels.mia: Let's do a fast recap of everything we have learnt in this chapter!
levels.body:
Here are the most important facts to remember:

• Perimeter = boundary length (units: cm, m)
• Area = surface covered (units: cm², m²)
• Rectangle perimeter = 2 × (l + b)
• Square perimeter = 4 × side
• Rectangle area = l × b
• Square area = side × side

Example: Remembering "perimeter is a length, area is a surface" helps you instantly pick the right unit — cm for perimeter, cm² for area.

check.q: Tap to check: is 'square metre' a unit of perimeter or area?
check.answer: Area — any unit written with a small 2 (like m² or cm²) always measures area, not perimeter.

levels.miaWin: Great recap! Your memory of this chapter is getting strong! 🎉

levels.title: True or False Practice
levels.mia: True/False questions are a great way to check if you really understand a fact, or just remember it partly!
levels.body:
Read each statement carefully and decide if it is completely true, or if some part of it is wrong.

Example statement: "The perimeter of a square with side 5 cm is 20 cm." Check: 4 × 5 = 20. This is TRUE.
Example statement: "The area of a rectangle 6 cm by 4 cm is 20 cm²." Check: 6 × 4 = 24, not 20. This is FALSE.
💡 Tip: Never guess on True/False — always recalculate quickly using the formula to check.

check.q: Tap to think: is this statement true or false: 'The perimeter of a rectangle 5 cm by 3 cm is 16 cm'?
check.answer: True — Perimeter = 2 × (5+3) = 2 × 8 = 16 cm, which matches the statement.

levels.miaWin: You are becoming an expert fact-checker! ⭐

levels.title: Fill in the Blanks Practice
levels.mia: Fill-in-the-blank questions test whether you remember the exact formula or word needed.
levels.body:
For fill-in-the-blank questions, first identify what is being asked (a formula, a unit, or a definition), then recall the exact fact.

Example: "The formula for the area of a square is side × ____." Answer: side (since Area = side × side).
Example: "Perimeter is measured in units of ____, while area is measured in ____ units." Answer: length; square.
💡 Tip: Whenever you see a blank about units, ask yourself: is this about a boundary (length) or a surface (square units)?

check.q: Tap to try: fill in the blank — 'The perimeter of a regular polygon = number of sides × ____.'
check.answer: length of one side (since all sides of a regular polygon are equal).

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You have completed the full Mensuration recap! 🚀

levels.title: Why Do We Need Algebra?
levels.mia: Hi! I'm Mia 🦊 Get ready for a brand-new chapter: Algebra! It's where maths starts using letters, not just numbers.
levels.body:
Look at this pattern of dots: 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 ... Every time, we add 2 to get the next number. Instead of writing this rule in words again and again, algebra lets us write it ONCE using a letter.

In algebra, a letter like n can stand for any number. So instead of saying 'a number added to itself gives double the number' every time, we simply write n + n = 2n — and this is true for every possible value of n!

Example: Whatever number you pick — 4, 10, or 100 — adding it to itself always doubles it: 4+4=8, 10+10=20, 100+100=200. Algebra writes this ONE idea as n + n = 2n.

check.q: Tap to think: in the rule n + n = 2n, can n be replaced by ANY number?
check.answer: Yes! That is the whole point of algebra — n stands for any number you choose, and the rule stays true every time.

levels.miaWin: Great start! You've just discovered why algebra is so powerful! 🎉

levels.title: Letters Stand for Numbers
levels.mia: In algebra, a letter isn't a mystery code — it's just a stand-in for a number we don't want to fix yet!
levels.body:
Suppose one pencil costs ₹5. If you buy 2 pencils, you pay ₹10. If you buy 7 pencils, you pay ₹35. Instead of calculating this fresh every time, we can let n stand for 'the number of pencils bought'. Then the cost of n pencils is always 5 × n, written as 5n.

Example: If a notebook costs ₹12, then the cost of b notebooks is 12b. When b=6, cost = 12×6 = ₹72.
💡 Tip: We usually write 5n instead of 5×n — in algebra, a number written right next to a letter means multiplication.

check.q: Tap to check: if one ticket costs ₹8, how would you write the cost of t tickets?
check.answer: 8t (which means 8 × t) — the cost of t tickets is always 8 times t.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You now know how to let a letter represent a changing number! ⭐

levels.title: Algebra All Around Us
levels.mia: Once you start noticing it, algebra is hiding behind rules everywhere — in shapes, patterns, and everyday life!
levels.body:
Algebra is a powerful tool because ONE general rule, written with letters, can replace THOUSANDS of separate number sentences.

Example: The rule 'Perimeter of a square = 4 × side' works for a square of ANY size — side 2 cm, 20 cm, or 2000 cm — without ever needing a new rule.
💡 Tip: Whenever you see a rule that should work for 'any number' or 'any shape', that is a perfect place for algebra!

check.q: Tap to think: why is a rule written with letters more useful than writing out lots of separate examples?
check.answer: Because a rule with letters (like 4l for a square's perimeter) works for every possible value at once, instead of needing a new sentence for every single case.

levels.miaWin: Excellent! You can now spot algebra hiding in the world around you! 🚀

levels.title: Building Patterns with Matchsticks
levels.mia: Let's build a growing pattern using matchsticks and find its algebra rule!
levels.body:
Look at this pattern of the letter 'L' made from matchsticks. Each L uses exactly 2 matchsticks. If we make n letter-Ls in a row (not joined), we need 2 matchsticks for each one.

Example: For n letter-Ls, the number of matchsticks needed = 2 × n = 2n. So 10 Ls need 2×10 = 20 matchsticks.

check.q: Tap to think: using the rule 2n, how many matchsticks are needed for 15 letter-Ls?
check.answer: 2 × 15 = 30 matchsticks.

levels.miaWin: Great! You found your first matchstick pattern rule! 🎉

levels.title: Patterns That Start With Extra Sticks
levels.mia: Some patterns don't start from zero — they need a few extra sticks at the very beginning too!
levels.body:
Now look at a row of squares made from matchsticks, where each new square shares one side with the previous one. The first square needs 4 matchsticks. But each NEW square after that only needs 3 more (since one side is already shared).

Example: For n joined squares: 1st square = 4 sticks, each of the remaining (n−1) squares adds 3 more sticks. Total = 4 + 3(n−1) = 3n + 1. Check for n=3: 3×3+1 = 10 ✓ (matches the picture!)
💡 Tip: Always test your rule on a small pattern you can count by hand, to make sure it gives the right answer.

check.q: Tap to check: using the rule 3n + 1, how many matchsticks are needed for 5 joined squares?
check.answer: 3 × 5 + 1 = 15 + 1 = 16 matchsticks.

levels.miaWin: Wonderful! You can now handle patterns with a 'starting extra' too! ⭐

levels.title: Finding the Rule Yourself
levels.mia: The best way to find a pattern's rule is to make a table and look for what changes each time!
levels.body:
Look at a chain of triangles made with matchsticks, each new triangle sharing one side with the one before. The first triangle needs 3 sticks; every triangle after that needs only 2 more sticks.

Example: The rule for this triangle chain is matchsticks = 2n + 1. For 8 triangles: 2×8+1 = 17 matchsticks.

check.q: Tap to try: using matchsticks = 2n + 1, how many matchsticks make a chain of 12 triangles?
check.answer: 2 × 12 + 1 = 24 + 1 = 25 matchsticks.

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You can now discover the algebra rule behind ANY growing pattern! 🚀

levels.title: What is a Variable?
levels.mia: You've been using letters like n already — now let's learn their proper name: variables!
levels.body:
A variable is a letter (like x, y, n, or l) that can take different numerical values — it is not stuck to one fixed number. In the matchstick rule 2n+1, the letter n is a variable: it can be 1, 2, 3, 4 ... and the total changes each time.

Example: In the expression x + 3, x is a variable. If x=2, the expression gives 5. If x=10, it gives 13 — the value of the expression changes because the value of the variable changes.

check.q: Tap to think: in the expression y − 4, is y a fixed number or a variable?
check.answer: y is a variable — it can take different values, and each different value of y gives a different result for y − 4.

levels.miaWin: Great! You now know exactly what a variable is! 🎉

levels.title: Variables vs Constants
levels.mia: Not everything in an expression changes — some parts always stay exactly the same!
levels.body:
A constant is a fixed number that never changes, like 5, 10, or −3. A variable changes value. In the expression 3x + 7: x is the variable, 3 is called the coefficient (it multiplies the variable), and 7 is a constant.

Example: In 5m − 2, m is the variable, 5 is the coefficient of m, and −2 is the constant term.

check.q: Tap to check: in the expression 8y + 1, which part is the constant?
check.answer: 1 is the constant — it stays the same no matter what value y takes.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You can now tell variables and constants apart! ⭐

levels.title: Common Variable Letters
levels.mia: Any letter can be a variable — but some are used so often, they've become maths favourites!
levels.body:
By convention (common agreement), we often use x, y, z, n for general numbers, and l, b, h, a for specific quantities in geometry (length, breadth, height, side). But this is just a habit — mathematically, ANY letter can be used as a variable.

Example: We write l for length and b for breadth in the rectangle rule 2(l+b), but we could equally use p and q — the LETTER doesn't matter, only what it represents.
💡 Tip: A variable letter is just a label — 'l' does NOT mean the word 'length' itself, it stands for a NUMBER (the length's value).

check.q: Tap to think: could you use the letter k instead of x to mean 'a number' in an expression?
check.answer: Yes — any letter works as a variable. k + 5 means exactly the same idea as x + 5, just with a different label.

levels.miaWin: Excellent! You're now fluent in the language of variables! 🚀

levels.title: Perimeter of a Square Using a Variable
levels.mia: Remember perimeter from the last chapter? Let's write its rule using algebra!
levels.body:
A square has 4 equal sides. If we call the length of one side l, then the perimeter (total boundary) is l + l + l + l, which we write shorter as 4l.

Example: If a square's side l = 9 cm, then its perimeter = 4l = 4×9 = 36 cm — using the SAME rule 4l for any square.

check.q: Tap to think: using the rule 4l, what is the perimeter of a square with side l = 15 cm?

levels.miaWin: Great! You've written your first algebraic geometry rule! 🎉

levels.title: Perimeter of a Rectangle Using Variables
levels.mia: A rectangle has two different side lengths, so its rule needs two letters!
levels.body:
A rectangle has length l and breadth b. Its perimeter is l + b + l + b, which simplifies to 2l + 2b, or even shorter: 2(l + b).

Example: A rectangular garden has l = 12 m and b = 7 m. Perimeter = 2(l+b) = 2(12+7) = 2×19 = 38 m.
💡 Tip: 2l + 2b and 2(l+b) always give the SAME answer — they are just two ways of writing the same rule.

check.q: Tap to check: using 2(l+b), what is the perimeter of a rectangle with l = 20 cm and b = 10 cm?

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You can now write the rectangle's rule from memory! ⭐

levels.title: Perimeter of an Equilateral Triangle
levels.mia: An equilateral triangle has all three sides equal — so its rule is just as neat as the square's!
levels.body:
If an equilateral triangle has each side equal to a, its perimeter is a + a + a, written as 3a. This is the same idea we used for the square (4l), just with 3 equal sides instead of 4.

Example: A road sign is an equilateral triangle with side a = 18 cm. Its perimeter = 3a = 3×18 = 54 cm.
💡 Tip: Any regular polygon's perimeter rule is 'number of sides × side length' — algebra lets us write ALL of these rules using letters: 3a for a triangle, 4l for a square, 5a for a pentagon, and so on.

check.q: Tap to think: what algebraic rule gives the perimeter of a regular pentagon with side s?
check.answer: 5s — since a regular pentagon has 5 equal sides, perimeter = 5 × s.

levels.miaWin: Wonderful! You can now write geometry rules for any regular shape! 🚀

levels.title: Commutativity of Addition
levels.mia: Here's a rule you've secretly known since Class 1 — now let's write it properly using algebra!
levels.body:
Try 4 + 7 and 7 + 4. Both equal 11! This works for ANY two numbers — adding them in either order gives the same sum. Using variables a and b, we write this general rule as: a + b = b + a.

Example: This rule works for every pair of numbers: 15 + 3 = 18 and 3 + 15 = 18 — always equal, no matter which number comes first.

check.q: Tap to think: using a + b = b + a, if a = 25 and b = 9, what does b + a equal?
check.answer: 34 — because a + b = 25 + 9 = 34, and b + a must give the exact same answer, 34.

levels.miaWin: Great! You've written your first arithmetic rule in algebra! 🎉

levels.title: Commutativity of Multiplication
levels.mia: Multiplication has the same 'order doesn't matter' magic as addition!
levels.body:
Try 3 × 5 and 5 × 3. Both equal 15! Using variables, this general rule is written as: a × b = b × a, or simply ab = ba.

Example: A rows-and-columns array: 4 rows of 6 chairs has the same total as 6 rows of 4 chairs — both give 24 chairs. That's ab = ba in action!
💡 Tip: Both a+b=b+a and ab=ba are true for ALL numbers — these are called the commutative rules of addition and multiplication.

check.q: Tap to check: using ab = ba, if a = 12 and b = 5, what is b × a?
check.answer: 60 — since a × b = 12 × 5 = 60, and b × a must also equal 60.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You now know both commutative rules! ⭐

levels.title: General Rules Save Words
levels.mia: Imagine writing 'the sum of two numbers stays the same in any order' every single time — algebra saves us all that writing!
levels.body:
The sentence 'For any two numbers, adding them in either order gives the same result' is long. Algebra shortens it to just a + b = b + a — a few symbols instead of many words, true for every number pair at once.

But be careful: NOT every operation works this way! Subtraction and division are NOT commutative — order DOES matter for them.

Example: a − b is NOT always equal to b − a. Check: 9−4=5, but 4−9=−5. They are different! So a−b ≠ b−a in general.

check.q: Tap to think: is division commutative? Check with 20 ÷ 4 and 4 ÷ 20.
check.answer: No — 20÷4=5, but 4÷20=0.2. Since these are different, division is NOT commutative; order matters.

levels.miaWin: Excellent! You now understand which rules always work and which don't! 🚀

levels.title: Building Simple Expressions
levels.mia: Now let's learn to turn everyday phrases into algebra using variables and operations!
levels.body:
An algebraic expression combines a variable with numbers using operations like +, −, ×, ÷. For example, 'a number x increased by 5' becomes x + 5, and 'a number y decreased by 3' becomes y − 3.

Example: 'Twice a number m' becomes 2m. 'A number p divided by 4' becomes p/4.

check.q: Tap to think: how would you write '8 more than a number n' as an expression?
check.answer: n + 8 — take the number n and add 8 to it.

levels.miaWin: Great start! You're now writing your own algebraic expressions! 🎉

levels.title: Expressions with Two Operations
levels.mia: Sometimes an expression needs TWO steps — a multiplication AND an addition or subtraction!
levels.body:
The expression 3x + 7 means: first multiply x by 3, then add 7. The expression 2y − 5 means: first multiply y by 2, then subtract 5.

Example: 'A number p is multiplied by 4, then 2 is subtracted' becomes 4p − 2.

check.q: Tap to check: how would you write 'a number x is multiplied by 5, then 3 is added' as an expression?
check.answer: 5x + 3 — first multiply x by 5, then add 3.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You can now build two-step expressions confidently! ⭐

levels.title: Translating Word Phrases into Expressions
levels.mia: Let's practise translating trickier phrases — the ORDER of words matters a lot in algebra!
levels.body:
Watch out for phrases where the operation comes in an unusual order. 'A number subtracted FROM 10' means 10 − x (not x − 10!). 'Twice a number decreased by 3' means 2x − 3.

Example: 'Sum of a number x and y' → x + y. 'The product of x and y, decreased by 5' → xy − 5.
💡 Tip: Read the phrase slowly and identify WHAT is being taken away FROM WHAT — that tells you the correct order for subtraction.

check.q: Tap to think: how would you write 'a number y subtracted from 20' as an expression?
check.answer: 20 − y — the number y is being taken away FROM 20, so 20 comes first.

levels.miaWin: Excellent! You can now translate tricky word phrases like an expert! 🚀

levels.title: Substituting a Value
levels.mia: An expression comes alive once you plug in a number for its variable — let's try it!
levels.body:
To find the value of an expression, replace the variable with a given number, then calculate. For x + 5, if x = 3, we substitute: 3 + 5 = 8.

Example: Find the value of y − 4 when y = 9. Substitute: 9 − 4 = 5.

check.q: Tap to think: what is the value of x + 10 when x = 7?

levels.miaWin: Great! You've found your first expression value! 🎉

levels.title: Expressions with Multiplication
levels.mia: When a variable is multiplied by a number, substitution still works the same way — just remember to multiply first!
levels.body:
For the expression 3x, if x = 4, substitute: 3 × 4 = 12. For 2x + 1, if x = 5, we first multiply, then add: 2×5 + 1 = 10 + 1 = 11.

Example: Find the value of 4m − 3 when m = 6. Substitute: 4×6 − 3 = 24 − 3 = 21.
💡 Tip: Always do the multiplication BEFORE the addition or subtraction when substituting values.

check.q: Tap to check: what is the value of 5y + 2 when y = 4?

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You can substitute into multi-step expressions now! ⭐

levels.title: Same Expression, Different Values
levels.mia: The exciting part of algebra: one expression can give a whole TABLE of different answers!
levels.body:
Watch how the expression 2x + 1 changes as x changes. This is exactly why algebra is powerful — one rule, many answers.

Example: As x goes 1, 2, 3, the value of 2x+1 goes 3, 5, 7 — increasing by 2 each time, just like x increases by 1 each time (2 × 1 = 2).

check.q: Tap to try: what is the value of 2x + 1 when x = 6?

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You now see how one expression creates many values! 🚀

levels.title: Age Problems
levels.mia: Let's use expressions to describe something very real — ages in a family!
levels.body:
Suppose Ravi's age is x years. If his father is 25 years older, the father's age is x + 25. If his younger sister is 4 years younger than Ravi, her age is x − 4.

Example: If Ravi's age x = 12, father's age = 12+25 = 37, sister's age = 12−4 = 8.

check.q: Tap to think: if a boy's age is x and his grandmother is 60 years older, what expression gives her age?
check.answer: x + 60 — since she is 60 years older, add 60 to his age.

levels.miaWin: Great! You've used algebra to describe a real family! 🎉

levels.title: Cost and Money Problems
levels.mia: Shops and markets use expressions like this every single day, even if they don't call it 'algebra'!
levels.body:
If one notebook costs ₹15, the cost of n notebooks is 15n. If you also buy one pen for a fixed ₹10, the TOTAL cost becomes 15n + 10.

Example: If n = 4 notebooks: Total cost = 15×4 + 10 = 60 + 10 = ₹70.
💡 Tip: Costs that repeat per item use multiplication (15n); one-time fixed costs are simply added on (+10).

check.q: Tap to check: using 15n + 10, what is the total cost for n = 6 notebooks?

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You can now model real shopping bills with algebra! ⭐

levels.title: Perimeter & Number Patterns Together
levels.mia: Let's combine everything — geometry rules, patterns, and expressions — in one real scenario!
levels.body:
Chairs are arranged around square tables placed in a row, and each table seats 4 people. For t tables placed separately (not joined), the total number of chairs needed is 4t.

Example: For a wedding hall with t = 20 separate square tables, chairs needed = 4×20 = 80 chairs.

check.q: Tap to think: using the rule 4t, how many chairs are needed for 35 tables?
check.answer: 4 × 35 = 140 chairs.

levels.miaWin: Excellent! You now use algebra to plan real events and situations! 🚀

levels.title: Expression vs Equation
levels.mia: Here's a big idea — an expression and an equation look similar but are actually quite different!
levels.body:
An expression (like x + 5) has NO equals sign — it just shows a calculation. An equation (like x + 5 = 12) HAS an equals sign, and says that two things are equal.

Example: 3y is an expression. 3y = 21 is an equation — it makes a claim that can be checked and solved.

check.q: Tap to think: is 2x − 3 an expression or an equation?
check.answer: An expression — it has no equals sign, so it is just a calculation, not a claim that two things are equal.

levels.miaWin: Great! You can now tell expressions and equations apart! 🎉

levels.title: LHS and RHS
levels.mia: Every equation has two sides — and they must always balance, just like a see-saw!
levels.body:
In an equation, the part BEFORE the equals sign is the LHS (Left Hand Side), and the part AFTER is the RHS (Right Hand Side). For the equation to be TRUE, LHS must equal RHS when the correct value is used.

Example: In 3y = 21, LHS = 3y and RHS = 21. When y=7, LHS = 3×7 = 21, which equals RHS — so the equation balances!
💡 Tip: Think of an equation like a balance scale — both sides must weigh the same for it to stay level.

check.q: Tap to check: in the equation 2m − 4 = 10, what is the LHS?
check.answer: 2m − 4 is the LHS, since it comes before the equals sign.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You understand how equations balance now! ⭐

levels.title: Checking if a Value Satisfies an Equation
levels.mia: How do we know if a guess for the variable is correct? We check by substituting it in!
levels.body:
To check if a value is a solution of an equation, substitute it into the LHS and see if it equals the RHS. If they match, the value is correct!

Example: Check if y = 4 satisfies 3y = 12. LHS = 3×4 = 12. RHS = 12. Since LHS = RHS, y = 4 IS the solution.

check.q: Tap to try: does x = 5 satisfy the equation x + 3 = 9?
check.answer: No — LHS = 5+3 = 8, but RHS = 9. Since 8 ≠ 9, x = 5 is NOT the solution.

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You can now check any equation like a detective! 🚀

levels.title: Solving by Trial and Error
levels.mia: The simplest way to solve an equation is to just try different numbers until it works!
levels.body:
To solve x + 4 = 10 by trial and error, try different values for x, and check each time whether LHS = RHS.

Example: Solve y − 2 = 5. Try y=6: 6−2=4 (too small). Try y=7: 7−2=5 ✓. So y = 7.

check.q: Tap to think: solve x + 3 = 9 by trying values. What is x?
check.answer: x = 6, because 6 + 3 = 9, which matches the RHS.

levels.miaWin: Great! You solved your first equation by trial and error! 🎉

levels.title: Guessing Smartly
levels.mia: Instead of guessing randomly, we can guess SMARTLY by thinking about whether we need a bigger or smaller number!
levels.body:
Solve 3x = 18. If a guess gives too small an LHS, try a BIGGER x next; if too big, try SMALLER. This narrows down the answer quickly.

Example: Solve 4y = 28. Try y=5: 20 (too small). Try y=7: 28 ✓. So y = 7.
💡 Tip: If your guess is too small, the next guess should be BIGGER — this helps you reach the answer in fewer tries.

check.q: Tap to check: solve 5x = 35 by smart guessing. What is x?
check.answer: x = 7, because 5 × 7 = 35, which matches the RHS.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You now solve equations quickly with smart guessing! ⭐

levels.title: Equations from Simple Rules
levels.mia: Let's combine everything — turn a statement into an equation, THEN solve it!
levels.body:
Statement: 'A number increased by 6 gives 14.' Step 1: Write the equation: x + 6 = 14. Step 2: Solve by trial: x = 8, since 8 + 6 = 14.

Example: 'Three times a number gives 21.' Equation: 3x = 21. Solve: x = 7.

check.q: Tap to try: form and solve the equation for 'a number decreased by 5 gives 9'.
check.answer: Equation: x − 5 = 9. Solving: x = 14, because 14 − 5 = 9.

levels.miaWin: Wonderful! You can now form AND solve your own equations! 🚀

levels.title: Turning Words into Equations
levels.mia: Every algebra word problem follows the same 4 steps — let's learn them once and use them forever!
levels.body:
Steps for solving an algebra word problem: (1) Identify the unknown quantity, (2) assign it a variable, (3) write an equation from the statement, (4) solve the equation.

Example: 'A number increased by 7 gives 15. Find the number.' Let the number be x. Equation: x + 7 = 15. Solving: x = 8.

check.q: Tap to think: what is the very first step in solving an algebra word problem?
check.answer: Identify the unknown quantity and give it a variable name (like x) — this is always the starting point.

levels.miaWin: Great! You now have a clear method for algebra word problems! 🎉

levels.title: Two-Step Word Problems
levels.mia: Some word problems need TWO operations in the equation — let's practise those!
levels.body:
Statement: 'Twice a number decreased by 4 is 10. Find the number.' Let the number be x. Equation: 2x − 4 = 10. Solve by trial: try x=7 → 2(7)−4 = 10 ✓. So x = 7.

Example: 'Three times a number, increased by 2, is 17.' Equation: 3x + 2 = 17. Solve: x = 5.
💡 Tip: Write the multiplication part first (since it usually applies to the whole 'number'), then the add/subtract part.

check.q: Tap to try: form and solve the equation for 'twice a number increased by 3 is 13'.
check.answer: Equation: 2x + 3 = 13. Solving: x = 5, because 2×5+3 = 13.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You can now handle two-step word problems! ⭐

levels.title: Real-Life Algebra Word Problems
levels.mia: Let's put it all together — age, cost, and perimeter problems, all solved the algebra way!
levels.body:
Statement: 'A rectangular garden has breadth 6 m. Its perimeter is 28 m. Find its length.' Let length = l. Equation: 2(l+6) = 28. Solve: l+6 = 14, so l = 8 m.

Example: 'Priya's age plus her brother's age (10 years) equals 24. Find Priya's age.' Equation: x + 10 = 24. Solve: x = 14 years.

check.q: Tap to think: 'The cost of a pen (₹6) and n pencils equals ₹36, with each pencil costing ₹5. Find n.'
check.answer: Equation: 6 + 5n = 36. So 5n = 30, giving n = 6 pencils.

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You've mastered real-life algebra word problems! 🚀

levels.title: Quick Recall — Key Facts
levels.mia: Let's do a fast recap of everything we have learnt in this chapter!
levels.body:
Here are the most important facts to remember:

• A variable is a letter that can take different values
• A constant is a fixed number that never changes
• An expression combines variables and numbers with operations, and has NO equals sign
• An equation has an equals sign: LHS = RHS
• Square perimeter = 4l; Rectangle perimeter = 2(l+b); Triangle perimeter = a+b+c
• a+b=b+a and ab=ba (commutative rules)

Example: Remembering 'expression = no equals sign, equation = has equals sign' instantly helps you classify any algebra statement.

check.q: Tap to check: is 5x − 2 an expression or an equation?
check.answer: An expression — it has no equals sign, so it is not making a claim of equality.

levels.miaWin: Great recap! Your memory of this chapter is getting strong! 🎉

levels.title: True or False Practice
levels.mia: True/False questions are a great way to check if you really understand a fact, or just remember it partly!
levels.body:
Read each statement carefully and decide if it is completely true, or if some part of it is wrong.

Example statement: 'The value of x + 3 when x = 5 is 8.' Check: 5+3 = 8. This is TRUE.
Example statement: 'a − b is always equal to b − a.' Check: 9−4=5, but 4−9=−5. These are different, so this is FALSE.
💡 Tip: Never guess on True/False — always substitute and recalculate quickly to check.

check.q: Tap to think: is this statement true or false: 'x = 4 is a solution of x + 6 = 10'?
check.answer: True — substituting x=4 gives 4+6=10, which matches the RHS exactly.

levels.miaWin: You are becoming an expert fact-checker! ⭐

levels.title: Fill in the Blanks Practice
levels.mia: Fill-in-the-blank questions test whether you remember the exact rule or word needed.
levels.body:
For fill-in-the-blank questions, first identify what is being asked (a rule, a definition, or a value), then recall the exact fact.

Example: 'The perimeter of an equilateral triangle with side a is ____.' Answer: 3a.
Example: 'In the expression 6x + 2, the constant term is ____.' Answer: 2.
💡 Tip: Whenever you see a blank about a shape's perimeter, ask yourself: how many equal or different sides does it have?

check.q: Tap to try: fill in the blank — 'The rule for the perimeter of a rectangle is 2 × ( ____ + ____ ).'
check.answer: length + breadth, written as l + b (since Perimeter = 2 × (l+b)).

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You have completed the full Algebra recap! 🚀

levels.title: What Are Numbers For?
levels.mia: Hi! I'm Mia 🦊 Ready to explore numbers with me? Let's start right from the beginning!
levels.body:
Numbers are all around us. We use them to count things (like how many pencils you have), to measure things (like your height or the time), and to compare things (like which bag is heavier).

Some numbers are small — easy to count quickly, like 1, 2, or 10. Others are large — much bigger, like 10,000 or 1,00,000.

Example: The number of students in your class (maybe 30 or 40) is a small number. The population of India (over 1,40,00,00,000 people!) is a large number.

check.q: Tap to see another example: is the number of pages in your maths notebook a small or large number?
check.answer: It's a small number — notebooks usually have only a few hundred pages at most, which is easy to count.

levels.miaWin: Nice! You're already thinking like a number explorer! 🎉

levels.title: Numbers Never End!
levels.mia: Here's something mind-blowing — there is no largest number in the world. Numbers just keep going... forever! ♾️
levels.body:
No matter how big a number you think of, you can always add 1 to make it even bigger. That means the list of numbers never has a final, biggest one — it just keeps going on and on.

This works for small numbers too — between any two numbers, there's always another number you could find.

Key Idea: 👉 There is no largest number — numbers go on forever. Even a number as huge as 1,00,00,00,000 (one hundred crore) isn't the biggest — just add 1!

check.q: Tap to think: If someone says "I know the biggest number ever," what could you say back?
check.answer: You could say: "Just add 1 to it — now THAT number is bigger!" Numbers never stop.

levels.miaWin: Exactly the kind of thinking a number explorer needs! 🚀

levels.title: Small vs Large — Spotting the Difference
levels.mia: Let's put it all together — here's how to quickly tell whether a number is small or large.
levels.body:
A simple way to tell: count the digits. Numbers with just 1-3 digits (like 5, 47, or 800) usually feel small and easy to picture in your head. Numbers with many more digits (like 50,000 or 12,34,567) are large — much harder to picture all at once.

Example: 10 (2 digits) feels small. 10,000 (5 digits) feels large. Both are valid numbers, but our brains experience them very differently!
💡 Tip: In your notebook, try writing 5 small numbers and 5 large numbers from things around you — it helps the idea stick!

check.q: Tap to check: between 1,00,000 and 10, which is the small number?
check.answer: 10 is the small number — it has far fewer digits than 1,00,000, which is a large number.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You're a numbers pro already! ⭐

levels.title: Step 1: Count the Digits
levels.mia: Time to compare numbers! My first trick — I always count the digits first. More digits means a bigger number, every time!
levels.body:
To compare numbers: Step 1 → the number with more digits is greater.

Example: 4567 > 3456 — wait, these have the SAME digit count, so we'd need Step 2! But comparing 4567 (4 digits) and 78,910 (5 digits): 78,910 is bigger.

check.q: Tap to see: which number is bigger — 9,876 or 10,001?
check.answer: 10,001 is bigger. It has more digits than 9,876, so it wins — even though it starts with a smaller-looking digit!

levels.miaWin: Nailed it! More digits = bigger number. 🦊
levels.miaTry: Remember my trick: count the digits first!

levels.title: Step 2: Same Digits? Go Left to Right
levels.mia: Now here's the tricky part — what if both numbers have the SAME number of digits? Then we compare from the left, just like reading a word!
levels.body:
If digit count is equal, compare the leftmost digits. If they match, move to the next digit, and so on.

Examples from your book:
• 4567 > 3456 (4 > 3 at the leftmost place)
• 78,910 > 78,109 (first three digits 7,8,9 match... wait — compare carefully: 78,910 vs 78,109 → at the 3rd digit, 9 > 1, so 78,910 wins)
💡 Tip: 👉 Always compare place values, left to right.

check.q: Tap to see: compare 5678 and 5768 — which is bigger?

To form the smallest number: arrange digits in ascending order (smallest first).

levels.title: The Indian System 🇮🇳
levels.mia: Did you know India and the rest of the world group big numbers differently? Let me show you the Indian way first!

Example: 12,345,678 is written the International way — commas every 3 digits!
💡 Key Difference: 👉 Commas are placed differently in each system!

levels.title: The Rounding Rule
levels.mia: Estimation is my favorite shortcut — it means finding a close, approximate value instead of the exact one!
levels.body:
The rounding rule is simple:

  • Digit 1–4 → Round DOWN
  • Digit 5–9 → Round UP
Examples from your book:
• 47 → 50 (round up)
• 42 → 40 (round down)

check.q: Tap to see: round 47 to the nearest 10.

levels.title: Choosing the Right Place Value

levels.body:
💡 Tip: 👉 Decide the place value first (tens, hundreds, or thousands) — that tells you which digit to check.

Example from your book: 4,117 → 4,100 (nearest hundred) or 4,000 (nearest thousand) — same number, different rounding targets!

check.q: Tap to see: round 345 to the nearest hundred.
check.answer: 300. The tens digit is 4 (1–4 range), so we round down: 345 → 300.

levels.title: Round to the Thousands
levels.mia: Let's go bigger — rounding to the nearest thousand!
levels.body:
For nearest thousand, check the hundreds digit. Same rule: 1–4 down, 5–9 up.

Practice Question: Round 6,789 to the nearest thousand.

levels.body:
To estimate a sum: round each number, then add the rounded numbers.

Example from your book: 5,290 + 17,986 ≈ 23,000

levels.title: Estimating Subtraction

To estimate a difference: round each number, then subtract.

Example from your book: 5,673 – 436 ≈ 5,300

check.q: Tap to see: estimate 5,673 − 436 (round first).
check.answer: About 5,300. Rounding 5,673 to 5,700 and 436 to 400, then 5,700 minus 400 = 5,300 — a quick, close estimate.

levels.title: Estimating Multiplication
levels.mia: Multiplication estimates are super handy for checking big calculations fast!
levels.body:
👉 Round BOTH numbers, then multiply the rounded values.

levels.title: The Basic Symbols
levels.mia: Ready for something ancient and cool? Romans wrote numbers using letters! Let's learn the basic symbols.
levels.body:
Basic Roman numeral symbols:

  • 1 = I

  • 10 = X
  • 50 = L

levels.title: Add or Subtract?
levels.mia: Here's the secret rule Romans used — where a smaller symbol sits tells you whether to ADD or SUBTRACT!
levels.body:
📌 Rules:

  • Smaller symbol AFTER bigger → ADD (VI = 5+1 = 6)
  • Smaller symbol BEFORE bigger → SUBTRACT (IV = 5−1 = 4)
Example: VI = 6, IV = 4 — same letters, different order, different number!

check.q: Tap to see: what number does IV represent?

levels.miaWin: 4! You cracked the add-or-subtract rule! 🔍

Examples from your book:
• 69 = LXIX

levels.title: What Are Whole Numbers?
levels.mia: Hi again! I'm Mia 🦊 Today we explore a brand-new family of numbers — whole numbers! Let's see how they're different from what you already know.
levels.body:
Natural numbers are the counting numbers: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5... If we add 0 to this list, we get whole numbers: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5...

Key Idea: Every natural number is a whole number, but 0 is a whole number that is NOT a natural number!

check.q: Tap to see: is 0 a natural number or a whole number?
check.answer: 0 is a whole number, but NOT a natural number. Natural numbers start from 1; whole numbers start from 0.

levels.miaWin: Exactly! That little 0 makes a big difference. 🎉

levels.title: Predecessor & Successor
levels.mia: Here's a fun pair of words — successor and predecessor. They just mean 'the next number' and 'the number before'!
levels.body:
The successor of a number is found by adding 1 to it. The predecessor is found by subtracting 1.

Example: Successor of 99 = 99 + 1 = 100. Predecessor of 100 = 100 − 1 = 99.
💡 Tip: 0 has NO predecessor, because there's no whole number before 0!

check.q: Tap to see: what is the successor of 999, and does 0 have a predecessor?
check.answer: The successor of 999 is 1,000. 0 has no predecessor, since whole numbers don’t go below 0.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! You've got predecessor and successor down. ⭐

levels.title: Whole Numbers on the Number Line
levels.mia: Now let's picture these numbers on a number line — it's like a ruler that goes on forever to the right!
levels.body:
On a number line, whole numbers are marked as points at equal distances, starting from 0 and going right: 0, 1, 2, 3...

The number on the left is always smaller, and the number on the right is always bigger.

0 to 9 on the number line — 7 sits to the right of 4, so 7 is bigger (7 > 4)
Example: On the number line, 7 is to the right of 4, so 7 > 4.

check.q: Tap to see: on a number line, is 15 to the left or right of 20, and what does that tell us?
check.answer: 15 is to the LEFT of 20 on the number line, which tells us 15 is smaller than 20 (15 < 20).

levels.miaWin: You're picturing numbers like a pro now! 🚀

levels.title: Adding on the Number Line
levels.mia: Let's use the number line as a tool! Adding numbers means hopping to the RIGHT.
levels.body:
To add two whole numbers on a number line, start at the first number, then jump to the right the number of times shown by the second number.

3 + 2 → start at 3, take 2 hops of 1 to the right, land on 5
Example: 3 + 2 → Start at 3, jump right 2 times → land on 5. So 3 + 2 = 5.

check.q: Tap to see: how would you show 4 + 3 on a number line?
check.answer: Start at 4, jump right 3 times (to 5, then 6, then 7) — you land on 7. So 4 + 3 = 7.

levels.miaWin: You're hopping like a pro! 🦘

levels.title: Subtracting on the Number Line
levels.mia: Subtraction is the opposite — instead of hopping right, we hop to the LEFT!
levels.body:
To subtract on a number line, start at the first number, then jump to the left the number of times shown by the second number.

6 − 4 → start at 6, take 4 hops of 1 to the left, land on 2
Example: 6 − 4 → Start at 6, jump left 4 times → land on 2. So 6 − 4 = 2.
💡 Tip: If you try to hop past 0 to the left, that subtraction doesn't give a whole number!

check.q: Tap to see: how would you show 8 − 5 on a number line?
check.answer: Start at 8, jump left 5 times (to 7, 6, 5, 4, then 3) — you land on 3. So 8 − 5 = 3.

levels.miaWin: Great hopping in the other direction! 🌟

levels.title: Why Some Subtractions Don't Work
levels.mia: Here's something tricky — sometimes subtraction on whole numbers just doesn't work out!
levels.body:
If you try to subtract a BIGGER number from a SMALLER one (like 3 − 7), you'd need to jump left past 0 — but there's nothing there in whole numbers!

3 − 7 needs 7 left-hops from 3, but whole numbers stop at 0 — there's no landing spot
Example: 3 − 7 would need 7 left-jumps from 3, landing at −4 — but −4 is not a whole number, so this subtraction isn't possible within whole numbers.

check.q: Tap to see: can you subtract 9 − 12 using only whole numbers?
check.answer: No — 9 − 12 would land at −3, which is not a whole number. Subtracting a bigger number from a smaller one doesn’t work within whole numbers.

levels.miaWin: Now you see why whole numbers have limits! 🔍

levels.title: Multiplying on the Number Line
levels.mia: Multiplication on a number line is like taking equal-sized jumps, again and again!
levels.body:
To multiply on a number line, start at 0, then take jumps of equal size, repeating it as many times as the second number says.

3 × 4 → start at 0, take 4 equal hops of size 3, land on 12
Example: 3 × 4 → Start at 0, take 4 jumps of size 3 → 0, 3, 6, 9, 12. You land on 12. So 3 × 4 = 12.

check.q: Tap to see: how would you show 2 × 5 on a number line?
check.answer: Start at 0, take 5 jumps of size 2: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. You land on 10. So 2 × 5 = 10.

levels.miaWin: You're jumping your way to multiplication mastery! 🎯

levels.title: Division as Repeated Subtraction
levels.mia: Here's a cool secret — division is just repeated subtraction! Let's see how that works on a number line.
levels.body:
To divide using a number line, start at the bigger number and keep jumping LEFT by the smaller number until you reach 0. Count how many jumps you made!

12 ÷ 3 → 4 hops of size 3 to the left lands exactly on 0, so 12 ÷ 3 = 4
Example: 12 ÷ 3 → Start at 12, jump left by 3 each time: 12→9→6→3→0. That's 4 jumps. So 12 ÷ 3 = 4.

check.q: Tap to see: how would you show 15 ÷ 5 on a number line?
check.answer: Start at 15, jump left by 5 each time: 15→10→5→0. That’s 3 jumps. So 15 ÷ 5 = 3.

levels.miaWin: You just discovered the secret link between division and subtraction! 🔓

levels.title: What If It Doesn't Land on 0?
levels.mia: Sometimes when we divide, our jumps don't land exactly on 0 — let's see what that means!
levels.body:
If repeated subtraction doesn't land exactly on 0, the division leaves a remainder — this means the division isn't exact.

10 ÷ 3 → 3 hops of size 3 land on 1, but a 4th hop would pass 0, so 10 ÷ 3 = 3 remainder 1
Example: 10 ÷ 3 → Start at 10, jump left by 3: 10→7→4→1. We can't jump left by 3 again without going past 0, so we stop at 1. That means 10 ÷ 3 = 3 with remainder 1.

check.q: Tap to see: what happens when you try 13 ÷ 4 using left-jumps on a number line?
check.answer: 13→9→5→1. We can’t jump left by 4 again without passing 0, so we stop at 1. That means 13 ÷ 4 = 3 with remainder 1.

levels.miaWin: You understand remainders now — that's an important discovery! 💡

levels.title: What Does 'Closure' Mean?
levels.mia: Today's word is 'closure' — sounds fancy, but it's a simple idea. Let's unlock it together!
levels.body:
A set of numbers is closed under an operation if doing that operation on any two numbers from the set ALWAYS gives an answer that's also in the set.

Adding 4 + 5 keeps the answer safely inside the whole-numbers pen, but 4 − 9 escapes it
Example: Whole numbers are closed under addition, because adding any two whole numbers ALWAYS gives another whole number — like 4 + 5 = 9 (still a whole number).

check.q: Tap to see: is the answer to 23 + 47 still a whole number?
check.answer: Yes — 23 + 47 = 70, which is a whole number. This confirms closure under addition.

levels.miaWin: You've unlocked the idea of closure! 🔓

levels.title: Closure Under Multiplication
levels.mia: Good news — multiplication behaves the same friendly way as addition!
levels.body:
Whole numbers are also closed under multiplication — multiplying any two whole numbers always gives another whole number.

Example: 6 × 7 = 42 — still a whole number! No matter which two whole numbers you multiply, you'll always land on a whole number.

check.q: Tap to see: is the answer to 12 × 9 still a whole number?
check.answer: Yes — 12 × 9 = 108, which is a whole number. Whole numbers are closed under multiplication.

levels.miaWin: Multiplication keeps it in the family too! 🎉

levels.title: NOT Closed Under Subtraction & Division
levels.mia: But here's the twist — subtraction and division don't always play by the same rules!
levels.body:
Whole numbers are NOT closed under subtraction or division, because sometimes the answer ISN'T a whole number.

Example: 5 − 9 = −4, which is NOT a whole number. And 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5, which is also NOT a whole number. So closure fails here!

check.q: Tap to see: does 3 − 8 give a whole number, and what does that tell us about closure?
check.answer: 3 − 8 = −5, which is not a whole number. This shows whole numbers are NOT closed under subtraction.

levels.miaWin: You've spotted the exception — that's sharp thinking! 🧠

levels.title: Order Doesn't Matter for Addition
levels.mia: Here's something you might already know without realizing it has a fancy name — let's call it the Commutative Property!
levels.body:
The commutative property of addition says: changing the ORDER of two numbers being added doesn't change the answer.

5 + 3 on one side of the scale, 3 + 5 on the other — the scale stays perfectly level
Example: 5 + 3 = 8, and 3 + 5 = 8 too! Same answer, different order.

check.q: Tap to see: does 12 + 7 give the same answer as 7 + 12?
check.answer: Yes! Both equal 19. This is the commutative property of addition in action.

levels.miaWin: Order doesn't matter — you've got it! 🔄

levels.title: Order Doesn't Matter for Multiplication Either
levels.mia: Guess what — multiplication has the same friendly rule!
levels.body:
The commutative property of multiplication says: changing the order of two numbers being multiplied doesn't change the answer.

Example: 4 × 6 = 24, and 6 × 4 = 24 too!

check.q: Tap to see: does 9 × 5 give the same answer as 5 × 9?
check.answer: Yes! Both equal 45. This is the commutative property of multiplication.

levels.miaWin: You've doubled your understanding of this property! ⭐

levels.title: Subtraction & Division Break the Rule
levels.mia: Here's the catch — subtraction and division do NOT follow this nice swapping rule!
levels.body:
For subtraction and division, swapping the order usually gives a DIFFERENT answer — so they are NOT commutative.

Example: 9 − 4 = 5, but 4 − 9 = −5 (not the same!). Also, 10 ÷ 2 = 5, but 2 ÷ 10 = 0.2 (also not the same!).

check.q: Tap to see: is 15 − 6 the same as 6 − 15?
check.answer: No — 15 − 6 = 9, but 6 − 15 = −9. They are different, showing subtraction is not commutative.

levels.miaWin: You've found the exception to the rule — great catch! 🔍

levels.title: Grouping Doesn't Matter for Addition
levels.mia: Let's explore another property — this one's about how we GROUP numbers when adding three or more!
levels.body:
The associative property of addition says: when adding three numbers, it doesn't matter which two you group together first — the answer stays the same.

Whichever pair you circle first and add, 2 + 3 + 4 always totals 9
Example: (2 + 3) + 4 = 5 + 4 = 9. And 2 + (3 + 4) = 2 + 7 = 9. Same answer either way!

check.q: Tap to see: does (1 + 5) + 2 give the same answer as 1 + (5 + 2)?
check.answer: Yes! Both equal 8. Grouping doesn’t change the sum — that’s the associative property.

levels.miaWin: Grouping doesn't matter — well discovered! 🎊

levels.title: Grouping Doesn't Matter for Multiplication
levels.mia: Multiplication follows this same grouping freedom too!
levels.body:
The associative property of multiplication says: when multiplying three numbers, the way you group them doesn't change the final answer.

Example: (2 × 3) × 4 = 6 × 4 = 24. And 2 × (3 × 4) = 2 × 12 = 24. Same answer!

check.q: Tap to see: does (5 × 2) × 3 give the same answer as 5 × (2 × 3)?
check.answer: Yes! Both equal 30. This confirms the associative property of multiplication.

levels.miaWin: Your grouping skills are excellent! 🌟

levels.title: Subtraction & Division Aren't Associative
levels.mia: Just like before, subtraction and division break this pattern too — let's see why!
levels.body:
For subtraction and division, changing the grouping usually gives a DIFFERENT answer, so they are NOT associative.

Example: (10 − 4) − 2 = 6 − 2 = 4. But 10 − (4 − 2) = 10 − 2 = 8. Different answers!

check.q: Tap to see: does (20 − 8) − 3 give the same answer as 20 − (8 − 3)?
check.answer: No — (20−8)−3 = 12−3 = 9, but 20−(8−3) = 20−5 = 15. They are different, showing subtraction is not associative.

levels.miaWin: You've uncovered another exception — sharp eyes! 👀

levels.title: Splitting Multiplication Over Addition
levels.mia: This property has a big name but a simple trick — it helps us split tricky multiplications into easier pieces!
levels.body:
The distributive property says: a × (b + c) = (a × b) + (a × c). Multiplying a sum is the same as multiplying each part and then adding.

Splitting 5 × (3 + 2) into 5×3 and 5×2 still gives the same total of 25 cookies
Example: 5 × (3 + 2) = 5 × 5 = 25. Also, (5 × 3) + (5 × 2) = 15 + 10 = 25. Same answer!

check.q: Tap to see: does 4 × (2 + 6) equal (4 × 2) + (4 × 6)?

levels.miaWin: You've cracked the distributive property! 🔑

levels.title: Using It for Easier Mental Maths
levels.mia: Here's why this property is so useful — it can make hard multiplication feel easy!
levels.body:
We can use the distributive property to break a tricky number into easier parts before multiplying.

Example: 7 × 102 = 7 × (100 + 2) = (7×100) + (7×2) = 700 + 14 = 714. Much easier than multiplying by 102 directly!

check.q: Tap to see: how would you use the distributive property to solve 6 × 103?

levels.miaWin: You're now using maths shortcuts like a pro! 🚀

levels.title: Distributive Property with Subtraction Too
levels.mia: Here's a bonus — this trick also works with subtraction inside the brackets!
levels.body:
The distributive property also works as: a × (b − c) = (a × b) − (a × c).

Example: 8 × (10 − 3) = 8 × 7 = 56. Also, (8×10) − (8×3) = 80 − 24 = 56. Same answer!

check.q: Tap to see: how would you use the distributive property to solve 9 × 98?

levels.miaWin: You can now distribute like a maths wizard! 🧙

levels.title: Spotting Number Patterns
levels.mia: Numbers love to follow patterns — once you spot one, maths gets a lot more fun!
levels.body:
A pattern is a sequence of numbers that follows a clear, repeating rule.

Example: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10... each number is 2 more than the one before — this is the pattern of even numbers.

check.q: Tap to see: what is the next number in the pattern 5, 10, 15, 20, ___?
check.answer: 25 — each number increases by 5, so the next one is 20+5=25.

levels.miaWin: You're a pattern detective now! 🔍

levels.title: Patterns with Shapes & Dots
levels.mia: Patterns aren't just numbers — we can build them using dots and shapes too!
levels.body:
Whole numbers can be shown as patterns of dots, like building squares or triangles.

Square numbers grow as bigger and bigger squares of dots: 1, 4, 9, 16, 25...
Example: Square numbers: 1, 4, 9, 16... can be shown as dots arranged in growing squares (1×1, 2×2, 3×3, 4×4).

check.q: Tap to see: what is the next square number after 16?
check.answer: 25, because it comes from 5×5 (the next square arrangement after 4×4=16).

levels.miaWin: You can see the shapes hiding inside numbers now! 🟦

levels.title: Using Patterns to Predict
levels.mia: The coolest part about patterns is that they help us predict numbers far ahead, without counting one by one!
levels.body:
Once you know the rule of a pattern, you can jump ahead and figure out numbers much further along — without listing every single one.

Example: In the pattern 3, 6, 9, 12... (multiples of 3), the 10th number would be 3×10=30, without writing out all 10 terms!

check.q: Tap to see: in the pattern 4, 8, 12, 16... (multiples of 4), what would the 8th number be?
check.answer: 32, because it is 4×8=32 — using the pattern’s rule instead of counting one by one.

levels.miaWin: You can now predict patterns like a true mathematician! 🎓

levels.title: What Is a Factor?
levels.mia: Hi! I'm Mia 🦊 New chapter, new ideas — let's meet factors and multiples, two best friends in the number world!
levels.body:
A factor of a number divides it EXACTLY, leaving no remainder.

12 dots arrange into a neat 3×4 grid (factors), but not into a neat grid of 5 (leftover dots, no clean rows)
Example: Factors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 — each one divides 12 exactly, with nothing left over.
💡 Tip: 1 is a factor of EVERY number, and every number is a factor of itself!

check.q: Tap to see: is 5 a factor of 20? Is 6 a factor of 20?
check.answer: 5 IS a factor of 20, since 20÷5=4 exactly. 6 is NOT a factor of 20, since 20÷6 leaves a remainder.

levels.miaWin: You've made your first factor-friends! 🎉

levels.title: What Is a Multiple?
levels.mia: Now let's flip it around — multiples are what you get when you multiply a number by 1, 2, 3, and so on!
levels.body:
A multiple of a number is what you get by multiplying it by any whole number (1, 2, 3...).

Example: Multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20... (4×1, 4×2, 4×3, 4×4, 4×5...) — they go on forever!
💡 Tip: Every number is a multiple of itself, and every multiple is always bigger than or equal to the number itself!

check.q: Tap to see: is 45 a multiple of 9? What about 50?
check.answer: 45 IS a multiple of 9, since 9×5=45. 50 is NOT a multiple of 9, since no whole number times 9 gives 50.

levels.miaWin: Multiples unlocked — you're on a roll! 🚀

levels.title: Factors vs Multiples — Don't Mix Them Up!
levels.mia: These two ideas sound similar, but they behave very differently — let's compare them side by side.
levels.body:
A number has only a limited number of factors (you can list them all), but it has unlimited multiples (they go on forever).

Example: Factors of 10: just 1, 2, 5, 10 (only 4 of them). Multiples of 10: 10, 20, 30, 40... (never-ending).

check.q: Tap to see: which has more entries — the list of factors of 18, or the list of multiples of 18?
check.answer: Multiples of 18 are endless (18, 36, 54...), while factors of 18 are a short, fixed list (1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18) — so multiples always "win" in number of entries.

levels.miaWin: You'll never mix up factors and multiples again! 🧠

levels.title: Quick Tests for 2, 5, and 10
levels.mia: Checking if a number divides exactly can take forever with long division — unless you know the secret shortcuts! Let's learn them.
levels.body:
A divisibility rule is a quick way to check if a number divides exactly into another, just by looking at its digits.

Only the LAST digit of 350 decides divisibility by 2, 5, and 10 — no need to check the rest!
Rule for 2: A number is divisible by 2 if its last digit is even (0,2,4,6,8). Rule for 5: last digit is 0 or 5. Rule for 10: last digit is 0.
💡 Tip: 350 ends in 0, so it's divisible by 2, 5, AND 10 — all three at once!

check.q: Tap to see: is 485 divisible by 2, by 5, or by both?
check.answer: 485 ends in 5, so it is divisible by 5, but NOT by 2 (since 5 is odd, not even).

levels.miaWin: You just learned 3 instant checks — no long division needed! ⚡

levels.title: Quick Tests for 3, 6, and 9
levels.mia: Now for a clever one — checking divisibility by 3 and 9 uses the DIGITS of the number, added together!
levels.body:
Rule for 3: add up all the digits — if the sum is divisible by 3, so is the original number. Rule for 9: same idea, but the digit sum must be divisible by 9. Rule for 6: the number must pass BOTH the rule for 2 AND the rule for 3.

Example: 126 → digits add to 1+2+6=9. Since 9 is divisible by both 3 and 9, so is 126! And since 126 is also even, it's divisible by 6 too.

check.q: Tap to see: is 234 divisible by 3? Is it divisible by 9?
check.answer: 2+3+4=9. Since 9 is divisible by both 3 and 9, 234 is divisible by both 3 and 9.

levels.miaWin: Adding digits to check divisibility — that's a real mathematician's trick! 🧮

levels.title: Quick Tests for 4, 8, and 11
levels.mia: A few more powerful shortcuts — these look at just the last couple of digits, or use a clever add-subtract pattern!
levels.body:
Rule for 4: check if the LAST TWO digits form a number divisible by 4. Rule for 8: check if the LAST THREE digits form a number divisible by 8. Rule for 11: add digits in odd positions, add digits in even positions, then subtract — if the result is 0 or divisible by 11, so is the number.

Example: 3,716 → last two digits are 16, and 16÷4=4 exactly, so 3,716 is divisible by 4!
