check.q: Tap to see: is 5,432 divisible by 4? (check the last two digits)
check.answer: Yes — the last two digits are 32, and 32÷4=8 exactly, so 5,432 is divisible by 4.

levels.miaWin: You now have a full toolkit of divisibility shortcuts! 🛠️

levels.title: What Makes a Number Prime?
levels.mia: Some numbers are quite picky about their factors — they only have two! Let's meet prime numbers.
levels.body:
A prime number has EXACTLY two factors: 1 and itself. It can't be divided exactly by any other number.

7 can only be arranged as a single row (1×7) — no other rectangle of dots is possible
Example: 7 is prime — its only factors are 1 and 7. Try dividing 7 by 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6 — none work exactly!
💡 Tip: 2 is the smallest prime number, and it's also the only EVEN prime number!

check.q: Tap to see: is 11 a prime number? What are its factors?
check.answer: Yes, 11 is prime. Its only factors are 1 and 11 — no other number divides it exactly.

levels.miaWin: You've spotted your first prime! ✨

levels.title: What Makes a Number Composite?
levels.mia: Now meet the opposite friend — composite numbers, who are happy to have lots of factors!
levels.body:
A composite number has MORE than two factors. It can be divided exactly by numbers other than just 1 and itself.

12 dots can be arranged as 2×6, 3×4, or 1×12 — many possible rectangles, so 12 is composite
Example: 12 is composite — its factors are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12 (six factors in total, not just two).
💡 Tip: 1 is special — it's neither prime NOR composite, because it has only ONE factor (itself)!

check.q: Tap to see: is 9 prime, composite, or neither? What about 1?
check.answer: 9 is composite (factors: 1, 3, 9 — three factors). 1 is neither prime nor composite, since it has only one factor.

levels.miaWin: You can now sort numbers like a true mathematician! 🗂️

levels.title: Finding Primes — The Sieve Idea
levels.mia: Want a clever trick to find all the prime numbers up to 100? Let's use the famous 'Sieve of Eratosthenes'!
levels.body:
To find primes up to a number, list all numbers, then cross out multiples of 2, 3, 5, 7... (but keep the number itself). Whatever is LEFT uncrossed is prime!

Example: From 2 to 20: cross out multiples of 2 (4,6,8...), then multiples of 3 (9,15...), then 5 (25 is beyond 20). What remains — 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19 — are all the primes up to 20!

check.q: Tap to see: using this method, is 17 prime? Is 18?
check.answer: 17 is prime — it survives the sieve since no smaller prime divides it exactly. 18 is composite — it gets crossed out as a multiple of 2 and 3.

levels.miaWin: You've just used a method mathematicians have trusted for 2,000+ years! 🏆

levels.title: Breaking Numbers into Prime Building Blocks
levels.mia: Here's something amazing — EVERY number can be broken down into a unique set of prime numbers multiplied together!
levels.body:
Prime factorization means writing a number as a product of ONLY prime numbers.

Example: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3 (all prime numbers!). No matter how you break 12 down, you'll always end up with these same primes.
💡 Tip: Primes are like the 'atoms' of numbers — every number is built from a unique combination of them!

check.q: Tap to see: what is the prime factorization of 18?
check.answer: 18 = 2 × 3 × 3 — breaking it down: 18=2×9, and 9=3×3, so all factors are prime: 2, 3, 3.

levels.miaWin: You've discovered the 'DNA' of numbers! 🧬

levels.title: The Factor Tree Method
levels.mia: The easiest way to find prime factorization is to draw a 'factor tree' — let's grow one together!
levels.body:
To build a factor tree: split the number into any two factors, then keep splitting each factor further until every branch ends in a prime number.

36 splits into 6 × 6, then each 6 splits into 2 × 3 — every leaf of the tree is a prime number
Example: 36 → split into 6 × 6 → each 6 splits into 2 × 3 → final primes: 2, 3, 2, 3. So 36 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 3.

check.q: Tap to see: using a factor tree, what is the prime factorization of 24?

levels.miaWin: Your factor tree is fully grown — and so is your skill! 🌳

levels.title: Repeated Division Method
levels.mia: Here's another neat way to find prime factors — keep dividing by the smallest prime that fits, again and again!
levels.body:
Start with the smallest prime (2), and keep dividing as long as it fits exactly. Move to the next prime (3, then 5, then 7...) when it stops fitting, until you reach 1.

Example: 60 ÷ 2 = 30 → 30 ÷ 2 = 15 → 15 ÷ 3 = 5 → 5 ÷ 5 = 1. The primes used were 2, 2, 3, 5. So 60 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.

check.q: Tap to see: using repeated division, what is the prime factorization of 45?

levels.miaWin: Two methods mastered — you can pick whichever feels easier! 🎯

levels.title: What Is HCF?
levels.mia: Time for two powerful tools — HCF and LCM! Let's start with HCF, the 'Highest Common Factor'.
levels.body:
The HCF (Highest Common Factor) of two numbers is the LARGEST number that divides both of them exactly.

Where the two circles overlap, you find the numbers shared by both lists — the biggest one is the HCF
Example: Factors of 12: 1,2,3,4,6,12. Factors of 18: 1,2,3,6,9,18. Common factors: 1,2,3,6 — the HIGHEST is 6. So HCF(12,18) = 6.

check.q: Tap to see: what is the HCF of 8 and 12?
check.answer: HCF(8,12) = 4. Factors of 8: 1,2,4,8. Factors of 12: 1,2,3,4,6,12. The highest common factor is 4.

levels.miaWin: You've found your first HCF! 🔑

levels.title: What Is LCM?
levels.mia: Now let's flip the idea — LCM stands for 'Lowest Common Multiple', the smaller cousin of HCF that deals with multiples instead!
levels.body:
The LCM (Lowest Common Multiple) of two numbers is the SMALLEST number that is a multiple of both.

Example: Multiples of 4: 4,8,12,16,20... Multiples of 6: 6,12,18,24... Common multiples: 12,24... The LOWEST is 12. So LCM(4,6) = 12.
💡 Tip: HCF is always the SMALLER (or equal) number, while LCM is always the BIGGER (or equal) number, compared to the original numbers!

check.q: Tap to see: what is the LCM of 3 and 5?
check.answer: LCM(3,5) = 15. Multiples of 3: 3,6,9,12,15... Multiples of 5: 5,10,15... The lowest common multiple is 15.

levels.miaWin: LCM mastered — you're building real number-power! ⚡

levels.title: HCF and LCM in Real Life
levels.mia: These ideas aren't just for textbooks — they help solve everyday puzzles too! Let's see how.
levels.body:
HCF helps when you need to split things into EQUAL, largest possible groups. LCM helps when you need to find when things will HAPPEN TOGETHER again.

Example: If a 12m rope and an 18m rope need to be cut into EQUAL pieces with no waste, the biggest piece size is the HCF: 6m. If two bells ring every 4 and 6 minutes, they'll ring together again after the LCM: 12 minutes.

check.q: Tap to see: two buses leave a stop every 15 minutes and every 20 minutes. After how many minutes will they leave together again?
check.answer: After 60 minutes — this is the LCM of 15 and 20. (Multiples of 15: 15,30,45,60... Multiples of 20: 20,40,60... First common one is 60.)

levels.miaWin: You can now use HCF and LCM to solve real puzzles! 🌟

levels.title: HCF Using Prime Factorization
levels.mia: Listing factors works fine for small numbers, but for bigger ones, prime factorization is much faster — let's see how!
levels.body:
To find HCF using prime factorization: break BOTH numbers into prime factors, then multiply only the primes that appear in BOTH lists (using the smaller power if repeated).

24 and 36 both contain two 2's and one 3 — multiplying just those shared primes gives the HCF, 12
Example: 24 = 2×2×2×3. 36 = 2×2×3×3. Common primes: 2×2 (both have at least two 2's) and one 3. So HCF = 2×2×3 = 12.

check.q: Tap to see: using prime factorization, what is the HCF of 18 and 30? (18=2×3×3, 30=2×3×5)
check.answer: Common primes are one 2 and one 3 (both numbers have at least these). HCF = 2×3 = 6.

levels.miaWin: You've leveled up your HCF skills with primes! 🔑

levels.title: LCM Using Prime Factorization
levels.mia: The same prime-factor trick works for LCM too — just with one small twist!
levels.body:
To find LCM using prime factorization: take EVERY prime that appears in either number, using the HIGHEST power it appears with, then multiply them all together.

Example: 12 = 2×2×3. 18 = 2×3×3. Take the highest power of each prime: 2×2 (from 12) and 3×3 (from 18). So LCM = 2×2×3×3 = 36.

check.q: Tap to see: using prime factorization, what is the LCM of 8 and 12? (8=2×2×2, 12=2×2×3)
check.answer: Highest power of 2 is 2×2×2 (from 8), and we also need the 3 (from 12). LCM = 2×2×2×3 = 24.

levels.miaWin: LCM by primes — fast and powerful! ⚡

levels.title: Why Prime Factorization Is Faster for Big Numbers
levels.mia: For small numbers, listing factors is easy. But what about huge numbers? That's where this method truly shines!
levels.body:
For large numbers, listing every factor takes a long time, but breaking into prime factors is quick and systematic — making HCF and LCM calculations much faster and less error-prone.

Example: Finding the HCF of 360 and 480 by listing ALL factors would take a while. But with prime factorization: 360=2×2×2×3×3×5 and 480=2×2×2×2×2×3. Common primes: 2×2×2×3 = 24. So HCF = 24 — found quickly!

check.q: Tap to see: why is prime factorization considered more reliable for very large numbers than listing all factors?
check.answer: Listing all factors of a large number can be slow and you might accidentally miss one, while breaking into primes follows a clear, repeatable process that’s harder to get wrong.

levels.miaWin: You now have a powerful method for ANY size of number! 🚀

levels.title: What Is a Point?
levels.mia: Hi! I'm Mia 🦊 New chapter — geometry! Everything in geometry starts with the simplest idea of all: a point. Let's begin!
levels.body:
A point marks an exact location. It has no length, width, or size — just a position. We mark it with a dot and name it using a capital letter, like A, B, or C.

Three separate points A, B, and C — each marks one exact location, with no size, width, or length at all
Example: If you touch a sharp pencil tip to paper, that tiny dot represents a point. Three different points might be labeled A, B, and C.
💡 Tip: A point only tells us WHERE something is — it has no actual size at all!

check.q: Tap to see: how many points are needed to mark a single exact location?
check.answer: Just one — a single point marks one exact location. We use more points only when we want to mark several locations.

levels.miaWin: You've placed your first point on the geometry map! 📍

levels.title: What Is a Line?
levels.mia: Now let's connect points! If we join two points and keep going forever in both directions, we get a line.
levels.body:
A line is a straight path of points that extends endlessly in BOTH directions. It has no endpoints and goes on forever. A line through points A and B is written as line AB (or line l).

Line AB passes through points A and B but extends infinitely in both directions — arrows on both ends show it never stops
Example: Imagine a perfectly straight road that never ends in either direction — that's like a line. We draw arrows on both ends to show it keeps going.
💡 Tip: A line has NO endpoints — it never stops, no matter which direction you travel!

check.q: Tap to see: does a line have a fixed length?
check.answer: No — a line goes on forever in both directions, so it has no fixed length. It is infinitely long.

levels.miaWin: Lines unlocked — straight and endless! ➖

levels.title: What Is a Line Segment?
levels.mia: A full line goes on forever, but sometimes we just want the part BETWEEN two points — that's a line segment!
levels.body:
A line segment is the shortest path connecting two FIXED points, called its endpoints. Unlike a line, it has a definite, measurable length. The segment from A to B is written as line segment AB.

A point has no size, a line has no endpoints, but a line segment has two fixed endpoints and a measurable length
Example: A ruler, a pencil, or the edge of a book are all like line segments — they have a clear start and a clear end, with a measurable length.
💡 Tip: Line : line segment :: endless road : a fixed-length fence between two posts!

check.q: Tap to see: what is the key difference between a line and a line segment?
check.answer: A line goes on forever in both directions with no endpoints, while a line segment has two fixed endpoints and a definite, measurable length.

levels.miaWin: You can now tell points, lines, and line segments apart like a pro! 📏

levels.title: What Is a Ray?
levels.mia: Here's a shape that's in between a line and a line segment — meet the ray!
levels.body:
A ray is a part of a line that starts at ONE fixed point (called the starting point or initial point) and goes on endlessly in only ONE direction.

Ray AB: starts at fixed point A, passes through B, and shoots onward forever — only one endpoint
Example: A beam of light from a torch, a flashlight, or sunlight streaming through a window are all like rays — they start at one point and travel onward in just one direction.
💡 Tip: A ray has exactly ONE endpoint (where it starts) but NO endpoint on the other side!

check.q: Tap to see: how many endpoints does a ray have?
check.answer: Just one — the starting point. The other direction goes on forever with no endpoint.

levels.miaWin: You've cast your first ray of geometric light! 🔦

levels.title: Naming Rays Correctly
levels.mia: Naming a ray has one important rule — let's make sure you never get it backwards!
levels.body:
A ray is named with its starting point FIRST, then any other point on it. Ray AB starts at A and passes through B, continuing endlessly past B. This is different from ray BA, which would start at B instead!

Ray AB starts at A and shoots through B to the right; Ray BA starts at B and shoots through A to the left — opposite directions!
Example: Ray PQ starts at P and goes through Q onward. Ray QP would start at Q and go through P onward — these point in OPPOSITE directions, even though they use the same two letters!

check.q: Tap to see: are ray AB and ray BA the same thing?
check.answer: No — ray AB starts at A and travels through B onward, while ray BA starts at B and travels through A onward. They point in opposite directions.

levels.miaWin: You'll never mix up a ray's direction again! ➡️

levels.title: Rays vs Lines vs Line Segments — All Together
levels.mia: Now that you know all three, let's compare them side-by-side so they never get confused again!
levels.body:
Line: no endpoints, goes on forever both ways. Ray: ONE endpoint, goes on forever one way. Line segment: TWO endpoints, has a fixed length.

All three side-by-side: a line has no endpoints, a ray has one, and a line segment has two — with a fixed length
Example: A railway track stretching to the horizon on both sides = a line. A flashlight beam = a ray. A matchstick = a line segment.

check.q: Tap to see: which of these three (line, ray, line segment) is the ONLY one with a fixed, measurable length?
check.answer: The line segment — since both a line and a ray extend forever in at least one direction, only the line segment has a fixed, measurable length.

levels.miaWin: Lines, rays, and segments — you've mastered all three! 🎓

levels.title: What Are Intersecting Lines?
levels.mia: When two lines meet, something interesting happens — let's see what we call that meeting point!
levels.body:
Intersecting lines are two or more lines that cross or meet at exactly one common point, called the point of intersection.

Two lines crossing form a giant X — they meet at exactly one shared point
Example: Picture a giant X shape — the two lines forming the X cross at one point in the middle. That crossing point is their point of intersection.
💡 Tip: Two straight lines (that aren't the same line) can cross at MOST one point!

check.q: Tap to see: if two lines cross each other, how many points of intersection do they have?
check.answer: Exactly one — two distinct straight lines can only cross at a single shared point.

levels.miaWin: You've spotted your first intersection! ✖️

levels.title: What Are Parallel Lines?
levels.mia: Now meet lines that NEVER meet, no matter how far they go — that's the magic of parallel lines!
levels.body:
Parallel lines are two or more lines in the same flat surface that never meet or cross, no matter how far they are extended in either direction. They always stay the same distance apart.

The two rails of a railway track stay exactly the same distance apart, no matter how far they extend
Example: The two rails of a railway track, the opposite edges of a ruler, or the lines on notebook paper are all examples of parallel lines.

check.q: Tap to see: will parallel lines ever touch if you extend them far enough?
check.answer: No — by definition, parallel lines never meet no matter how far they are extended; they always stay the same distance apart.

levels.miaWin: Parallel lines — forever side by side! 〛〛

levels.title: Spotting Intersecting vs Parallel in Real Life
levels.mia: Let's practice spotting both types of lines all around us — they're hiding in plain sight!
levels.body:
To tell them apart: if two lines (extended fully) would eventually cross, they're intersecting. If they stay the same distance apart forever, they're parallel.

Real-life examples: a + sign shows intersecting lines; notebook lines and door sides show parallel lines that never meet
Example: A plus sign (+) shows two intersecting lines crossing at the center. The two long sides of a door frame are parallel — they never meet.

check.q: Tap to see: are the two diagonals of a square (corner to corner) intersecting or parallel?
check.answer: Intersecting — both diagonals of a square cross each other at the exact center of the square.

levels.miaWin: You're spotting line relationships everywhere now! 👀

levels.title: What Is a Curve?
levels.mia: Time to leave straight lines behind for a moment — let's explore curves!
levels.body:
In geometry, a curve is any drawing made without lifting your pencil and without using a ruler. Surprisingly, even a straight line counts as a special type of curve!

A wavy line, a closed loop, and even a straight line are all 'curves' in geometry — the key is one unbroken stroke
Example: A wavy squiggle, a circle, a zigzag, and even a straight line are all curves — as long as you drew them in one continuous stroke.
💡 Tip: In everyday language, "curve" means "not straight" — but in maths, it includes straight lines too!

check.q: Tap to see: is a straight line considered a curve in geometry?
check.answer: Yes — in mathematics, any drawing made without lifting the pencil counts as a curve, including straight lines.

levels.miaWin: Curves: more flexible than you thought! 🌀

levels.title: Open Curves vs Closed Curves
levels.mia: Curves come in two main types depending on whether their ends meet — let's tell them apart!
levels.body:
A curve is closed if its starting and ending points meet up, forming a loop with no gaps. A curve is open if the ends do NOT meet.

An open curve's two ends stay apart; a closed curve's path joins back to where it started
Example: A circle or a square outline are CLOSED curves (the path joins back to where it started). A wavy letter "S" or a smile shape are OPEN curves (the ends don't connect).

check.q: Tap to see: is the letter “C” an open or closed curve?
check.answer: Open — the two ends of the letter C do not meet or join together.

levels.miaWin: Open or closed — you can tell at a glance now! 🔓🔒

levels.title: Simple Curves and Regions
levels.mia: Here's one more idea — closed curves create special regions inside and outside themselves. Let's see how!
levels.body:
A curve is simple if it doesn't cross itself. A simple closed curve divides the page into three parts: the interior (inside), the boundary (the curve itself), and the exterior (outside).

A simple closed curve splits the page into three zones: boundary (the curve), interior (inside), and exterior (outside)
Example: Draw a circle. Any point INSIDE it is in the interior, any point on the circle's edge is on the boundary, and any point OUTSIDE it is in the exterior.

check.q: Tap to see: how many regions does a simple closed curve divide a page into, and what are they called?
check.answer: Three regions: the interior (inside), the boundary (the curve itself), and the exterior (outside).

levels.miaWin: You've mapped out the regions of a closed curve perfectly! 🗺️

levels.title: What Is a Polygon?
levels.mia: Closed curves made ONLY of straight line segments have a special name — polygons! Let's meet them.
levels.body:
A polygon is a simple closed curve made ENTIRELY of line segments (no curved parts allowed). These line segments are called the sides of the polygon.

Triangles, squares, and hexagons are polygons — all straight sides. A circle is NOT a polygon because it has a curved boundary
Example: A triangle (3 sides), a square (4 sides), and a pentagon (5 sides) are all polygons — they're built only from straight line segments joined end to end.
💡 Tip: A circle is NOT a polygon, because it's made of a curve, not straight line segments!

check.q: Tap to see: why is a circle not considered a polygon?
check.answer: Because a polygon must be made entirely of straight line segments, while a circle is a curved shape with no straight sides.

levels.miaWin: You've entered the world of polygons! 🔷

levels.title: Vertices and Adjacent Sides
levels.mia: Every polygon has special meeting points and neighboring sides — let's learn their names!
levels.body:
The point where two sides of a polygon meet is called a vertex (plural: vertices). Two sides that share a common vertex are called adjacent sides.

Square ABCD: each corner is a vertex, and sides meeting at the same vertex (like AB and BC at B) are adjacent
Example: In a square ABCD, the corners A, B, C, D are its vertices. Sides AB and BC are adjacent because they share vertex B.

check.q: Tap to see: how many vertices does a hexagon (6-sided polygon) have?
check.answer: 6 vertices — a polygon always has the same number of vertices as it has sides.

levels.miaWin: Vertices and adjacent sides — locked in! 📐

levels.title: Naming Polygons by Number of Sides
levels.mia: Polygons get different names depending on how many sides they have — let's learn the most common ones!
levels.body:
3 sides = triangle. 4 sides = quadrilateral. 5 sides = pentagon. 6 sides = hexagon. The number of sides ALWAYS equals the number of vertices AND the number of angles in a polygon.

The number of sides decides the name — and it always equals the number of vertices and angles too
Example: A stop sign has 8 sides, making it an octagon. A honeycomb cell has 6 sides, making it a hexagon.

check.q: Tap to see: what do we call a polygon with 5 sides, and how many vertices does it have?
check.answer: A pentagon — and it has 5 vertices, since the number of vertices always matches the number of sides.

levels.miaWin: You can now name polygons by their sides like a geometry expert! 🏅

levels.title: What Is an Angle?
levels.mia: Whenever two rays share a starting point, something new is formed — an angle! Let's explore.
levels.body:
An angle is formed when two rays start from the SAME common point. The common starting point is called the vertex, and the two rays are called the arms (or sides) of the angle.

Rays OP and OQ share starting point O — the vertex — forming angle ∠POQ with an interior between the arms
Example: Rays OP and OQ, both starting at point O, form the angle ∠POQ (read as "angle POQ"). Notice the vertex O is always written in the MIDDLE when naming the angle.
💡 Tip: When naming an angle with three letters, the VERTEX always goes in the middle!

check.q: Tap to see: in angle ∠ABC, which letter represents the vertex?
check.answer: B — the middle letter in the angle’s name always represents the vertex.

levels.miaWin: You've formed your very first angle! 📐

levels.title: Interior, Exterior, and the Angle Itself
levels.mia: An angle actually divides the whole page into three separate zones — let's map them out!
levels.body:
An angle creates three regions: the angle itself (the two rays/arms), the interior (the region 'inside' the angle, between the arms), and the exterior (everything else outside).

The shaded region between the arms is the interior; everywhere else (light yellow) is the exterior; the arms themselves are the angle
Example: Imagine an angle like an open book. The pages themselves are the angle's arms, the gap between the pages is the interior, and the space around the book is the exterior.

check.q: Tap to see: if a point lies exactly on one of the rays forming an angle, is it in the interior, exterior, or on the angle itself?
check.answer: On the angle itself — points lying on either of the two arms are considered part of the angle, not the interior or exterior.

levels.miaWin: You've mapped all three regions of an angle! 🗺️

levels.title: Angles Sharing Points and Rays
levels.mia: Sometimes two different angles can share parts with each other — let's see how that works!
levels.body:
Two angles can share just their vertex (one common point), or they can share an entire arm/ray (one common ray), depending on how they're drawn.

Left: two angles share only the vertex O. Right: ∠AOB and ∠AOC share the common ray OA (dashed)
Example: If ray OA is shared between angle ∠AOB and angle ∠AOC, then both angles share ONE common ray (OA) and ONE common point (the vertex O).

check.q: Tap to see: if two angles share only their vertex (and no rays), how many common points do they have?
check.answer: Just one common point — the shared vertex — since none of their rays overlap.

levels.miaWin: You can now describe how angles relate to each other! 🔗

levels.title: What Is a Triangle?
levels.mia: The simplest possible polygon has a special place in geometry — let's meet the triangle!
levels.body:
A triangle is a polygon with exactly 3 sides, 3 vertices, and 3 angles. It is the polygon with the fewest possible sides. A triangle with vertices A, B, C is written as △ABC.

△ABC has 3 vertices (A, B, C), 3 sides (AB, BC, CA), and 3 angles — one at each vertex
Example: Triangle ABC has sides AB, BC, and CA, and angles ∠BAC, ∠ABC, and ∠BCA — three of each, formed by the three vertices A, B, and C.
💡 Tip: No polygon can have fewer than 3 sides — a triangle is the simplest shape that can enclose a region!

check.q: Tap to see: how many sides, vertices, and angles does every triangle have?
check.answer: Every triangle has exactly 3 sides, 3 vertices, and 3 angles.

levels.miaWin: You've built your first triangle! 🔺

levels.title: Interior, Exterior, and Sides of a Triangle
levels.mia: Just like angles and curves, triangles also have their own interior and exterior — let's explore.
levels.body:
A triangle, being a closed shape, has an interior (inside the triangle) and an exterior (outside the triangle). The three line segments forming it are the sides, and where any two sides meet is a vertex.

Triangle PQR divides the plane into three parts: interior (blue), the boundary/sides (the triangle), and exterior (yellow)
Example: In triangle PQR, a point exactly in the middle of the triangle lies in the interior, while a point far away outside the triangle's edges lies in the exterior.

check.q: Tap to see: how many vertices and how many sides does a triangle have in total?
check.answer: A triangle has 3 vertices and 3 sides — one side connects each pair of vertices.

levels.miaWin: Triangle regions, fully explored! 🔍

levels.title: Triangles Are Everywhere!
levels.mia: Triangles aren't just in textbooks — they show up constantly in the world around us. Let's spot a few!
levels.body:
Triangles are used in construction and design because their shape is very strong and stable — they don't easily bend out of shape compared to other polygons.

Triangles in the real world: bridge trusses, roof frames, and even pizza slices all use the triangle's natural strength and stability
Example: Bridges, roof trusses, and bicycle frames often use triangle shapes for extra strength. A slice of pizza or a traffic yield sign are everyday triangle shapes too!

check.q: Tap to see: why do builders often use triangle shapes in bridges and roofs?
check.answer: Because triangles are very stable and resist bending or collapsing under pressure, unlike shapes with more sides such as squares.

levels.miaWin: You'll spot triangles everywhere you look now! 🌉

levels.title: What Is a Quadrilateral?
levels.mia: One side more than a triangle, and you get a whole new family of shapes — quadrilaterals!
levels.body:
A quadrilateral is a polygon with exactly 4 sides, 4 vertices, and 4 angles. A quadrilateral with vertices A, B, C, D is written as quadrilateral ABCD, and its vertices must be named in order (going around the shape).

A square, rectangle, and trapezium are all quadrilaterals — each has exactly 4 sides, 4 vertices, and 4 angles
Example: Quadrilateral ABCD has sides AB, BC, CD, and DA. Going around in order matters — naming it ABCD is correct, but naming it ACBD (skipping around) would be wrong.

check.q: Tap to see: how many sides, vertices, and angles does every quadrilateral have?
check.answer: Every quadrilateral has exactly 4 sides, 4 vertices, and 4 angles.

levels.miaWin: You've discovered the world of quadrilaterals! 🔷

levels.title: Opposite Sides and Opposite Angles
levels.mia: Quadrilaterals have an interesting feature — sides and angles that face each other across the shape!
levels.body:
In quadrilateral ABCD: sides AB and CD are opposite sides (they don't share a vertex), and sides BC and DA are also opposite sides. Similarly, ∠A and ∠C are opposite angles, and ∠B and ∠D are opposite angles.

In quadrilateral ABCD: orange dashes = opposite sides (AB↔CD, BC↔AD); pink arcs = opposite angles (∠A↔∠C, ∠B↔∠D)
Example: In quadrilateral PQRS, side PQ is opposite to side RS, and angle P is opposite to angle R.

check.q: Tap to see: in quadrilateral WXYZ, which side is opposite to side WX?
check.answer: Side YZ — it does not share any vertex with WX, making it the opposite side.

levels.miaWin: Opposite sides and angles — fully understood! ↔️

levels.title: Diagonals and Adjacent Sides
levels.mia: Quadrilaterals have one more special feature — lines that cut across the inside of the shape!
levels.body:
A diagonal is a line segment that joins two OPPOSITE vertices of a quadrilateral (vertices that are not next to each other). Adjacent sides are two sides that DO share a common vertex.

Diagonals AC and BD connect opposite corners, cutting across the inside of quadrilateral ABCD
Example: In quadrilateral ABCD, the diagonals are AC and BD — they connect opposite corners. Sides AB and BC are adjacent because they share vertex B.

check.q: Tap to see: how many diagonals does a quadrilateral have in total?
check.answer: 2 diagonals — connecting each pair of opposite vertices (for ABCD, these are AC and BD).

levels.miaWin: You've mastered every part of a quadrilateral! 🏆

levels.title: What Is a Circle?
levels.mia: Time for a shape with NO straight sides at all, NO corners, and a very special property — the circle!
levels.body:
A circle is a simple closed curve made of all points that are the SAME fixed distance from one central point, called the centre. A circle is NOT a polygon, since it has no straight sides.

A circle: every point on the boundary (blue) is the same distance from centre O — that's what makes it perfectly round
Example: A wheel, a coin, or the rim of a cup are all circles — every point on their edge is exactly the same distance from the center.
💡 Tip: A circle has infinitely many points, all equally distant from its center — that's what makes it perfectly round!

check.q: Tap to see: why is a circle not classified as a polygon?
check.answer: Because a polygon must be made of straight line segments, while a circle is a curved shape with no straight sides or vertices.

levels.miaWin: You've drawn your first perfect circle! ⭕

levels.title: Radius and Diameter
levels.mia: Circles have two important measurements that describe their size — let's learn both!
levels.body:
The radius is a line segment joining the centre to ANY point on the circle. The diameter is a line segment that passes through the centre, connecting two points on opposite sides of the circle. The diameter is always TWICE the radius (d = 2r).

The radius runs from centre to edge; the diameter runs edge-to-edge through the centre, exactly twice as long
Example: If a circle has a radius of 5cm, its diameter is 2×5=10cm. The diameter is the longest line segment you can draw inside a circle.

check.q: Tap to see: if a circle has a diameter of 18cm, what is its radius?
check.answer: 9cm — since the diameter is always twice the radius, the radius is half the diameter: 18÷2=9.

levels.miaWin: Radius and diameter — fully measured! 📏

levels.title: Chord, Arc, Sector, and Segment
levels.mia: A circle has even more special parts hiding inside it — let's discover chords, arcs, sectors, and segments!
levels.body:
A chord is any line segment joining two points on the circle (the diameter is actually the LONGEST possible chord). An arc is a part of the circle's boundary. A sector is a 'pizza slice' region between two radii and an arc. A segment is the region between a chord and its arc.

A sector is a pizza-slice region between two radii; a segment is the region trapped between a chord and its arc
Example: A pizza slice from the center to the crust is a sector. The crust itself (the curved edge) is an arc. Cutting a circle with a straight knife cut (not through the center) creates a chord and a segment.

check.q: Tap to see: is the diameter of a circle also considered a chord?
check.answer: Yes — the diameter is a special chord that happens to pass through the centre, making it the longest possible chord of the circle.

levels.miaWin: You've explored every part of a circle like a true geometer! 🎯

levels.title: Comparing Line Segments
levels.mia: Hi! I'm Mia 🦊 Let's begin our shapes journey with the simplest building block of all — the line segment!
levels.body:
A line segment has two fixed endpoints, so it has a definite, fixed length — unlike a line, which goes on forever in both directions.

We can compare two line segments in three ways: by observation (just looking — works only when the difference is huge), by tracing (placing one on top of the other), and by using a ruler and a divider (the most accurate way).

Comparing two line segments by observation — CD is clearly longer than AB
Example: Looking at your pencil and your geometry box, you can instantly tell the geometry box's edge is longer — that's comparison by observation.

check.q: Tap to see: why can't we always trust comparison by observation alone?
check.answer: Because when two line segments are close in length, our eyes can be fooled — we need a ruler or divider for an accurate comparison.

levels.miaWin: Great start — you can now compare line segments like a pro! 📏

levels.title: Measuring with a Ruler
levels.mia: Now let's learn the most common way to measure a line segment — using a ruler!
levels.body:
To measure a line segment with a ruler: place the ruler along the segment, read the mark at the starting point, read the mark at the ending point, and subtract the smaller reading from the larger reading.

Reading a ruler: end mark (8) minus start mark (2) = length (6 cm)

check.q: A line segment starts at the 3cm mark and ends at the 9cm mark. How long is it?
check.explain: Length = ending mark − starting mark = 9 − 3 = 6cm.

levels.miaWin: You're reading rulers like an expert now! 🎯
levels.miaTry: No worries — remember, always subtract the smaller reading from the bigger one!

levels.title: Measuring with a Divider (More Accurate)
levels.mia: Rulers can have a small error if your eye isn't perfectly aligned. Let's learn the more accurate way — using a divider!
levels.body:
A divider has two pointed, adjustable legs. To measure a line segment, open the divider so its two points exactly match the two endpoints of the segment. Then, WITHOUT changing the opening, lift the divider and place it on a ruler to read off the length.

Example: Using a divider avoids the error of looking at the ruler from an angle (called the 'angle of vision' error), which can happen when reading a ruler directly against a curved or uneven object.
💡 Tip: A divider is especially useful for measuring a line segment that is drawn on a curved surface, or for comparing two segments without a ruler at all — just open the divider to match one, then check it against the other!

check.q: Fill in the blank: A ____ has two pointed legs and is used for very accurate measurement of line segments.
check.answer: divider
check.explain: A divider’s two adjustable pointed legs let us copy a length exactly and transfer it to a ruler for a precise reading.

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You now know all 3 ways to measure and compare line segments! 🏆

levels.title: What Is an Angle?
levels.mia: Two rays sharing a starting point create something very important in geometry — an angle! Let's explore.
levels.body:
An angle is formed when two rays meet at a common endpoint, called the vertex. The two rays are called the arms of the angle. Angles are measured in degrees (°), using a tool called a protractor.

The orange ray swings open from the blue ray, sweeping out the angle at the vertex
Example: The two hands of a clock form an angle at the centre — as the minute hand moves, the angle between the hands changes.

check.q: Tap to see: what are the two rays of an angle called?
check.answer: The arms of the angle. The point where they meet is called the vertex.

levels.miaWin: You've discovered your first angle! 📐

levels.title: The Right Angle as a Benchmark
levels.mia: There's one special angle that we use as a reference point for naming all others — the right angle. Let's see why it matters!
levels.body:
A right angle measures exactly 90° — it looks like a perfect corner, such as the corner of a book or a square tile. A straight angle measures exactly 180° — its two arms point in exactly opposite directions, forming a straight line. A complete angle (full turn) measures 360°.

A right angle (90°, a perfect corner) compared to a straight angle (180°, a straight line)

check.q: How many right angles (90°) make up one straight angle (180°)?
check.explain: 180° ÷ 90° = 2 — two right angles placed together make a straight angle.

levels.miaWin: Right angles, straight angles, complete angles — you've got the benchmarks down! 🧭

levels.title: Acute, Obtuse, and Reflex Angles
levels.mia: Now let's classify ALL angles using the right angle (90°) and straight angle (180°) as our measuring sticks!
levels.body:
An acute angle is SMALLER than 90° (between 0° and 90°). An obtuse angle is BIGGER than 90° but SMALLER than 180°. A reflex angle is BIGGER than 180° but smaller than 360° — it's the 'outside' part of an angle, more than a straight line's worth of turn.

An angle smaller than 90° (between the dashed line and the orange ray) is acute
Example: A slice of pizza usually forms an acute angle at the tip. An open laptop screen often forms an obtuse angle with its base. The angle a clock's hands make going the 'long way round' past 6 o'clock can be a reflex angle.

check.q: An angle measures 110°. What type of angle is it?
check.explain: 110° is more than 90° but less than 180°, so it is an obtuse angle.

levels.miaWin: You can now classify any angle just by its measure — amazing work! 🏆

levels.title: Meet the Protractor
levels.mia: We know HOW to classify angles by sight, but now let's learn to measure them EXACTLY, using a protractor!
levels.body:
A protractor is a semi-circular tool marked from 0° to 180°. To measure an angle: place the protractor's centre point exactly on the angle's vertex, line up the base line (0°) with one arm of the angle, then read the scale where the other arm crosses it.

The orange arm sweeps across the protractor's scale — wherever it stops is the angle's measure

check.q: Tap to see: what is the FIRST step when using a protractor?
check.answer: Place the protractor’s centre point exactly on the vertex of the angle you want to measure, lining up its base line with one arm.

levels.miaWin: You're ready to measure any angle with confidence! 📐

levels.title: Reading the Scale Correctly
levels.mia: Protractors have TWO scales running in opposite directions — this trips up a lot of students! Let's make sure you never get confused.
levels.body:
Most protractors have two rows of numbers: one going 0° → 180° left to right, and another going 180° → 0° left to right (right to left). You must read from the SAME side where you placed the 0° base line — always start counting from the arm that lines up with 0° on your chosen scale.

💡 Tip: If one arm of the angle lines up with the LEFT 0°, read using the scale that starts at 0° on the left. If it lines up with the RIGHT 0°, use the scale starting at 0° on the right!
Example: If an arm lines up with the left 0° mark, and the other arm crosses the inner scale at 50, the angle is 50° — NOT the outer scale's 130, since that belongs to the other 0° mark.

check.q: If you place the base line at the LEFT 0° mark, which scale should you read?
opts: The scale that starts at 0° on the left
The scale that starts at 0° on the right
Either scale — they always give the same answer
check.explain: Always read the scale matching the same 0° mark where you placed your base line, or you'll get the wrong angle.

levels.miaWin: Reading protractor scales correctly — that's the trickiest part mastered! 🎯
levels.miaTry: Don't worry, this confuses many students at first — just remember to match your 0° starting point!

levels.title: Drawing an Angle of a Given Measure
levels.mia: Now that you can measure angles, let's flip it around — let's DRAW an angle of an exact measure using a protractor!
levels.body:
To draw an angle of, say, 60°: draw a ray (one arm) first. Place the protractor's centre on the ray's starting point (vertex), with the base line along the ray. Find the 60° mark on the correct scale, and make a small dot there. Remove the protractor and join the vertex to the dot — that's your 60° angle!

Example: To draw a 45° angle, after marking the dot at 45°, draw a straight ray from the vertex through that dot using your ruler.

check.q: Fill in the blank: After marking the dot at the correct angle measure, you join the ____ to the dot using a ruler to complete the angle.
check.answer: vertex
check.explain: You draw a straight ray from the vertex through the marked dot to complete the angle of the required measure.

levels.miaWin: You can now both measure AND construct any angle — true geometry mastery! 🏆

levels.title: What Are Perpendicular Lines?
levels.mia: Right angles show up everywhere once you know to look — and perpendicular lines are where they live! Let's explore.
levels.body:
Two lines are perpendicular to each other if they intersect (cross) and form a right angle (90°) at the point where they meet. We write 'line AB is perpendicular to line CD' using the symbol ⊥: AB ⊥ CD.

The orange line settles into place at exactly 90° to the blue line — that's perpendicularity
Example: The vertical and horizontal edges of a window frame, or the two edges meeting at the corner of a notebook page, are perpendicular to each other.

check.q: Tap to see: what angle MUST two lines form to be called perpendicular?
check.answer: Exactly a right angle, 90° — that is the defining condition for perpendicular lines.

levels.miaWin: You've spotted your first pair of perpendicular lines! ⊥

levels.title: The Perpendicular Bisector
levels.mia: There's a special perpendicular line that does something extra — it cuts a segment exactly in half too! Let's meet it.
levels.body:
A perpendicular bisector of a line segment is a line that is BOTH perpendicular to the segment AND passes through its midpoint (cutting it into two exactly equal halves). It satisfies two conditions at once: a 90° angle AND equal division.

The orange line crosses at exactly the midpoint, at exactly 90° — both conditions met at once

check.q: What TWO conditions must be true for a line to be a perpendicular bisector of a segment?
opts: It must be parallel and equal in length
It must cross at 90° AND pass through the midpoint
It must just touch one endpoint
check.explain: A perpendicular bisector must be perpendicular (90°) to the segment AND pass exactly through its midpoint.

levels.miaWin: You now understand one of geometry's most useful special lines! 🌟

levels.title: Identifying Perpendicularity in Real Life
levels.mia: Perpendicular lines aren't just on paper — let's spot them in the world around us!
levels.body:
Many everyday structures rely on perpendicular lines for strength and stability. Walls meeting the floor, the lines of a tic-tac-toe (noughts and crosses) grid, and the spokes of certain wheel designs often include perpendicular relationships.

💡 Tip: Not every pair of crossing lines is perpendicular! Two lines can intersect at an acute or obtuse angle too — perpendicularity ONLY happens when that angle is exactly 90°.

check.q: Fill in the blank: Two crossing lines are called perpendicular ONLY if the angle between them is exactly ____ degrees.
check.explain: Crossing lines are perpendicular only when they meet at exactly 90° — any other angle means they are simply "intersecting," not perpendicular.

levels.miaWin: You can now spot perpendicular lines anywhere you look! 🏆

levels.title: Classifying Triangles by Sides
levels.mia: Triangles can be sorted in TWO different ways — by their sides, or by their angles. Let's start with sides!
levels.body:
By their SIDES, triangles are classified as: Equilateral (all 3 sides equal), Isosceles (exactly 2 sides equal), and Scalene (all 3 sides different lengths).

Watch the left triangle morph between Equilateral and Scalene — equal-length sides change the shape's name
Example: A slice of a perfectly square sandwich cut corner to corner is isosceles (2 equal sides). A traffic warning sign is usually equilateral.

check.q: Tap to see: which type of triangle has NO equal sides at all?
check.answer: A scalene triangle — all three of its sides have different lengths.

levels.miaWin: You can now classify triangles by their sides! 🔺

levels.title: Classifying Triangles by Angles
levels.mia: Now let's classify triangles a SECOND way — using their angles. Remember our angle types from before? They come back here!
levels.body:
By their ANGLES, triangles are: Acute-angled (all 3 angles acute, i.e. each less than 90°), Right-angled (one angle is exactly 90°), and Obtuse-angled (one angle is obtuse, i.e. more than 90°). Recall: acute means under 90°, obtuse means between 90° and 180° — these same definitions now describe a triangle's angles too.

The right-angled triangle's 90° corner pulses — spot it by the perfect square corner
💡 Tip: A triangle can NEVER have two right angles or two obtuse angles — the three angles always add up to exactly 180°, so there's only ever room for ONE angle of 90° or more!

check.q: A triangle has angles 50°, 60°, and 70°. What type is it (by angle)?
check.explain: All three angles (50°, 60°, 70°) are less than 90°, so it is an acute-angled triangle.

levels.miaWin: Two classification systems, fully understood! 🎯

levels.title: Combining Both Classifications
levels.mia: Here's a fun twist — a single triangle gets BOTH a side-name AND an angle-name at the same time! Let's see how they combine.
levels.body:
Every triangle has both a side-based name and an angle-based name simultaneously. For example, a triangle could be an isosceles right-angled triangle (2 equal sides, one 90° angle) — both descriptions apply to the same shape at once!

Example: An equilateral triangle (all sides equal) is ALWAYS acute-angled too, because all its angles are automatically equal at 60° each (since 180°÷3=60°), and 60° is less than 90°.

check.q: Fill in the blank: An equilateral triangle’s three angles are always equal, each measuring ____ degrees.
check.explain: Since the three angles of any triangle add up to 180°, and an equilateral triangle’s three angles are all equal, each one measures 180° ÷ 3 = 60°.

levels.miaWin: You've mastered triangle classification completely — both by sides AND angles! 🏆

levels.title: What Is a Quadrilateral?
levels.mia: From three-sided triangles, let's move up to FOUR-sided shapes — quadrilaterals are everywhere, from doors to phone screens!
levels.body:
A quadrilateral is a closed figure with exactly 4 sides, 4 vertices (corners), and 4 angles. The sum of the interior angles of any quadrilateral is always 360° — exactly double a triangle's 180°!

The four orange vertices pulse in turn — count them to confirm it's a quadrilateral
Example: A phone screen, a door, a book cover, and a chessboard square are all quadrilaterals.

check.q: Tap to see: what do the four interior angles of ANY quadrilateral always add up to?
check.answer: 360° — exactly double the 180° angle sum of a triangle.

levels.miaWin: You now know the basic rule behind EVERY 4-sided shape! 🟦

levels.title: Special Quadrilaterals — Squares, Rectangles & Parallelograms
levels.mia: Not all quadrilaterals are the same — some have extra-special properties! Let's meet the most common ones.
levels.body:
A parallelogram has both pairs of opposite sides parallel and equal. A rectangle is a parallelogram with all four angles equal to 90°. A square is a rectangle with all four sides equal too — it's the most special of all!

Watch the left shape morph between Square and Rectangle — equal sides make all the difference

check.q: What makes a rectangle different from a general parallelogram?
opts: It has parallel sides (same as any parallelogram)
All four of its angles are exactly 90°
check.explain: A rectangle is a special parallelogram where ALL four angles equal exactly 90°.

levels.miaWin: Squares, rectangles, parallelograms — you've sorted the family tree! 🌳

levels.title: Rhombus and Trapezium
levels.mia: Two more important quadrilaterals to add to your collection — the rhombus and the trapezium!
levels.body:
A rhombus is a parallelogram with all 4 sides equal in length (but its angles don't have to be 90°, so it can look 'tilted', like a diamond). A trapezium has only ONE pair of opposite sides parallel (not both pairs).

The rhombus tilts back and forth — all 4 sides stay equal even as the angles change
💡 Tip: A square is ALSO a rhombus (all sides equal) AND a rectangle (all angles 90°) at the same time — it sits at the top of the family, inheriting properties from both!

check.q: Fill in the blank: A trapezium has only ____ pair of opposite sides parallel (not both pairs).
check.answer: one
check.explain: A trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel opposite sides, unlike a parallelogram which has both pairs parallel.

levels.miaWin: You now know the full quadrilateral family — square, rectangle, parallelogram, rhombus, and trapezium! 🏆

levels.title: What Is a Polygon?
levels.mia: Triangles and quadrilaterals are actually part of a much BIGGER family of shapes called polygons. Let's zoom out and see the full picture!
levels.body:
A polygon is any closed figure made of straight line segments only (no curves). Polygons are named by their number of sides: triangle (3), quadrilateral (4), pentagon (5), hexagon (6), heptagon (7), and octagon (8).

From triangle to hexagon — the hexagon gently pulses as the side-count keeps growing
Example: A stop sign is an octagon (8 sides). A honeycomb cell is a hexagon (6 sides). A soccer ball's white panels are pentagons (5 sides).

check.q: Tap to see: what is the ONE key rule that makes a shape a polygon?
check.answer: It must be a closed figure made ENTIRELY of straight line segments — no curves allowed anywhere in its boundary.

levels.miaWin: You now know the whole polygon family, from triangle to octagon! 🔷

levels.title: Regular vs Irregular Polygons
levels.mia: Polygons can be neat and symmetric, or wonky and uneven — let's learn the difference!
levels.body:
A regular polygon has ALL sides equal AND all angles equal (like a perfect hexagon). An irregular polygon has sides and/or angles that are NOT all equal — it can look lopsided or stretched.

The irregular hexagon wobbles slightly — its sides and angles are clearly not matching, unlike its regular twin

check.q: What defines a REGULAR polygon?
opts: All sides AND all angles are equal
check.explain: A regular polygon requires BOTH equal side lengths AND equal angles throughout.

levels.miaWin: Regular and irregular — you can now spot the difference instantly! 🎯

levels.title: Counting Sides, Angles, and Diagonals
levels.mia: Here's something cool — for ANY polygon, the number of sides ALWAYS equals the number of angles AND the number of vertices!
levels.body:
For any polygon: number of sides = number of vertices = number of angles. For example, a hexagon (6 sides) always has exactly 6 vertices and 6 angles. A diagonal is a line segment connecting two non-adjacent vertices (corners that aren't already joined by a side).

💡 Tip: A triangle has ZERO diagonals — because every pair of its 3 vertices is already directly connected by a side! Diagonals only start appearing once a polygon has 4 or more sides.
Example: A quadrilateral has exactly 2 diagonals (connecting each pair of opposite corners). A pentagon has 5 diagonals.

check.q: Fill in the blank: A polygon with 6 sides always has exactly ____ vertices.
check.explain: For any polygon, the number of sides always equals the number of vertices.

levels.miaWin: Sides, vertices, angles, and diagonals — you've mastered the building blocks of every polygon! 🏆

levels.title: Faces, Edges, and Vertices
levels.mia: Time to step out of flat shapes into the 3rd dimension! Every solid shape is built from 3 key parts — let's learn to spot each one.
levels.body:
Every 3D (solid) shape has: faces (the flat or curved surfaces), edges (the line segments where two faces meet), and vertices (the corner points where edges meet). A cuboid, for example, has 6 faces, 12 edges, and 8 vertices.

Watch each part of the cuboid highlight in turn — faces, then edges, then a vertex
Example: A dice (cube) has 6 square faces, 12 edges, and 8 vertices (corners) — try counting them on a real dice!

check.q: Tap to see: what are the THREE basic parts every solid (3D) shape has?
check.answer: Faces (flat or curved surfaces), edges (where two faces meet), and vertices (corner points where edges meet).

levels.miaWin: You can now identify the building blocks of any 3D shape! 📦

levels.title: Common 3D Shapes — Cube, Cuboid, and Cylinder
levels.mia: Let's meet some everyday 3D shapes and count their faces, edges, and vertices one by one!
levels.body:
A cube has 6 equal square faces, 12 equal edges, and 8 vertices (like a dice). A cuboid has 6 rectangular faces (not all equal), 12 edges, and 8 vertices (like a brick or a box). A cylinder has 2 flat circular faces and 1 curved surface, with NO straight edges or vertices in the usual sense (like a can of soda).

The cylinder gently pulses, reminding us its curved surface has no sharp edges or vertices at all

check.q: How many faces, edges, and vertices does a cube have?
check.explain: A cube has 6 equal square faces, 12 edges, and 8 vertices.

levels.miaWin: Cube, cuboid, cylinder — you can now count their parts with confidence! 🎯

levels.title: Cone, Sphere, and Pyramid
levels.mia: Three more important 3D shapes to round out your collection — let's finish strong!
levels.body:
A cone has 1 flat circular face, 1 curved surface, and 1 vertex (the pointed tip). A sphere (like a ball) has just 1 curved surface — no flat faces, no edges, and no vertices at all! A pyramid (like the Egyptian pyramids) has a flat polygon base plus triangular faces meeting at a single top vertex.

Each shape’s special vertex (or lack of one) pulses gently — spheres alone have none at all
💡 Tip: A sphere is the ONLY common 3D shape with NO flat faces, NO straight edges, and NO vertices — it's entirely curved, like a ball!

check.q: Fill in the blank: A sphere has zero flat faces, zero edges, and zero ____.
check.answer: vertices
check.explain: A sphere is entirely curved with no flat faces, straight edges, or corner vertices at all.

levels.miaWin: You've explored the full world of 3D shapes — faces, edges, vertices, and all! 🏆

levels.title: What Are Integers?
levels.mia: Hi! I'm Mia 🦊 Get ready to meet a brand new family of numbers — integers — that include numbers BELOW zero too!
levels.body:
Integers are the collection of whole numbers AND their negatives: ...,−3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3,... Positive integers are greater than zero, negative integers are less than zero, and zero itself is neither positive nor negative.

Zero glows at the centre — everything to its left is negative, everything to its right is positive
Example: A temperature of 5°C below zero is written as −5. A profit of ₹200 is +200, while a loss of ₹200 is −200.

check.q: Tap to see: is zero a positive integer, a negative integer, or neither?
check.answer: Zero is neither positive nor negative — it sits exactly at the boundary between the two groups.

levels.miaWin: You've just met the integers — numbers both above AND below zero! ➖➕

levels.title: Using the + and − Signs
levels.mia: Every integer (except zero) needs a sign to show whether it's positive or negative. Let's learn how to read and write them correctly.
levels.body:
A positive integer is written with a '+' sign (often left out, since plain numbers are assumed positive) — so 5 means +5. A negative integer MUST always be written with a '−' sign, like −5. The sign tells us the integer's direction from zero.

Same '3 floors', opposite signs — the + or − tells you which direction from ground level (zero)
💡 Tip: The negative sign is NEVER optional! Writing '5' instead of '−5' completely changes the number's meaning — always double-check the sign before reading or writing any integer.
Example: A lift going 3 floors UP from the ground floor is at +3. A lift going 3 floors DOWN into the basement is at −3.

check.q: A submarine is 150m below sea level. How should this depth be written as an integer?
check.explain: Since the submarine is BELOW sea level (the zero point), its position is written as the negative integer −150.

levels.miaWin: Signs sorted! You can now read and write integers correctly. ✅

levels.title: Integers in Real Life
levels.mia: Integers aren't just a math exercise — they describe real situations all around us, every single day!
levels.body:
Integers help us describe quantities that can go in two opposite directions from a starting point (zero): temperature above/below freezing, money earned/spent, floors above/below ground, distance gained/lost in a game, and altitude above/below sea level.

Both heights are integers measured from the same zero point — sea level
Example: Mount Everest's peak is about +8,849m (above sea level). The Mariana Trench's deepest point is about −10,935m (below sea level). Both are integers describing height relative to sea level (zero).

check.q: Fill in the blank: A team loses 7 yards in American football. As an integer, this is written as ____.
check.explain: Losing yards moves backward from the starting point, so it is written as the negative integer −7.

levels.miaWin: You can now spot integers hiding in everyday life — money, height, temperature, and more! 🏆

levels.title: Plotting Integers
levels.mia: The number line is the perfect map for integers — let's learn to place any integer exactly where it belongs!
levels.body:
On a number line, integers are marked at equal distances apart. Zero sits at the centre, positive integers extend to the RIGHT, and negative integers extend to the LEFT. To plot an integer, simply count that many equal steps from zero in the correct direction.

The orange token hops from 0 to +3, three equal steps to the right
Example: To plot −4, start at 0 and count 4 equal steps to the LEFT.

check.q: Tap to see: which direction do POSITIVE integers go on a number line?
check.answer: Positive integers extend to the RIGHT of zero; negative integers extend to the LEFT.

levels.miaWin: You can now plot any integer exactly where it belongs! 📍

levels.title: Distance from Zero
levels.mia: Here's something neat — integers that are EQUAL distances from zero come in opposite-sign pairs!
levels.body:
The distance of an integer from zero (ignoring its sign) is the number of steps between them. +5 and −5 are both exactly 5 steps from zero — they are called opposite integers. Every integer (except 0) has exactly one opposite.

−5 and +5 sit at equal but opposite distances from zero, both arcs pulsing together

check.q: What is the opposite of the integer −8?
check.explain: The opposite of −8 is +8 (written simply as 8) — same distance from zero, opposite direction.

levels.miaWin: Opposite integers, mastered! Every integer has its perfect mirror partner. 🪞

levels.title: Comparing Positions on the Number Line
levels.mia: The number line doesn't just show WHERE integers are — it instantly tells us which is bigger or smaller too!
levels.body:
On a number line, an integer further to the RIGHT is always GREATER than an integer to its LEFT — no matter if both are positive, both negative, or one of each. This single rule works for ALL integers.

−3 sits to the right of −7, so −3 is the greater integer, even though both are negative
💡 Tip: This means EVERY positive integer is greater than EVERY negative integer, and among negative integers, the one with the smaller 'size' (closer to zero) is actually the GREATER one! For example, −2 is greater than −5, because −2 is further right.

check.q: Fill in the blank: Between −3 and −7, the GREATER integer is ____.
check.explain: −3 is further to the right on the number line than −7, so −3 is the greater integer.

levels.miaWin: You can now compare ANY two integers instantly using the number line! 🏆

levels.title: Adding Using the Number Line
levels.mia: Adding integers is like taking HOPS on the number line! Let's learn the simple direction rule.
levels.body:
To add integers on a number line: start at the FIRST number. If adding a POSITIVE integer, hop to the RIGHT that many steps. If adding a NEGATIVE integer, hop to the LEFT that many steps. Where you land is the answer!

Starting at 1, the token hops 2 steps to the right (since we're adding a positive 2), landing on 3
Example: To find 2 + (−5): start at 2, then hop 5 steps LEFT (since we're adding a negative), landing on −3. So 2 + (−5) = −3.

check.q: Tap to see: which direction do you hop when adding a NEGATIVE integer?
check.answer: You hop to the LEFT — the same number of steps as the negative integer’s value.

levels.miaWin: You can now add integers using hops on the number line! 🦘

levels.title: Adding Two Integers with the SAME Sign
levels.mia: When both integers point the SAME way, adding them is simple — just add their sizes and keep the sign!
levels.body:
To add two POSITIVE integers: add their values normally — the answer is positive. To add two NEGATIVE integers: add their values (ignoring signs), then put a NEGATIVE sign on the answer.

Two same-direction hops simply add up — the answer keeps that shared direction (sign)
Example: 4 + 7 = 11 (both positive, so the answer is positive). (−4) + (−7): add 4 and 7 to get 11, then make it negative: −11.
💡 Tip: When signs match, think of it as combining two debts or two gains — they just pile up together in the SAME direction!

check.explain: Add the values (6+9=15), then keep the negative sign since both integers were negative: −15.

levels.miaWin: Same-sign addition is now easy for you! ➕➖

levels.title: Adding Two Integers with DIFFERENT Signs
levels.mia: What happens when a positive and a negative integer add together? They actually CANCEL each other out, partly!
levels.body:
To add two integers with DIFFERENT signs: SUBTRACT the smaller value from the bigger value (ignoring signs), and give the answer the sign of whichever original integer had the BIGGER value (ignoring signs).

The −4 hop cancels 4 of the +9 gain, leaving a smaller positive answer of +5
Example: 9 + (−4): the bigger value (ignoring signs) is 9, which is positive. Subtract: 9−4=5. Since 9 was positive, the answer is +5. So 9 + (−4) = 5.
Example: (−10) + 3: the bigger value (ignoring signs) is 10, which is negative. Subtract: 10−3=7. Since 10 was negative, the answer is −7. So (−10) + 3 = −7.

check.q: What is (−12) + 5?
check.explain: The bigger value (ignoring signs) is 12, which is negative. 12−5=7, and since 12 was negative, the answer is −7.

levels.miaWin: You've mastered adding integers in EVERY situation — same signs and different signs! 🏆

levels.title: Additive Inverse — The Integer That Cancels You Out
levels.mia: Every integer has a secret partner that, when added to it, always gives ZERO. Let's meet the additive inverse!
levels.body:
The additive inverse (also called the negative or opposite) of an integer is the integer you must add to it to get 0. The additive inverse of a is −a, and the additive inverse of −a is a. In other words, a + (−a) = 0.

−6 and its additive inverse +6 are mirror images across zero — added together they cancel out completely
Example: The additive inverse of 9 is −9, since 9 + (−9) = 0. The additive inverse of −15 is 15, since (−15) + 15 = 0. The additive inverse of 0 is 0 itself.
💡 Tip: To find the additive inverse of ANY integer, just flip its sign — that's it! Positive becomes negative, negative becomes positive, and zero stays zero.

check.q: What is the additive inverse of −23?
check.explain: Flip the sign: the additive inverse of −23 is 23, because (−23) + 23 = 0.

levels.miaWin: You've found every integer's perfect cancel-partner — the additive inverse! 🔄

levels.title: The Big Secret: Subtracting = Adding the Opposite
levels.mia: Here's the BIGGEST shortcut in all of integer math — subtracting an integer is secretly the SAME as adding its opposite!
levels.body:
To subtract an integer, change the subtraction into addition by using the OPPOSITE of the integer being subtracted: a − b = a + (−b). This turns every subtraction problem into an addition problem you already know how to solve!

Subtracting 5 becomes adding −5: the token hops LEFT 5 times, starting from 3, landing on −2
Example: 8 − 3 becomes 8 + (−3) = 5. Both give the same familiar answer — but now you can use the SAME addition rules for every subtraction!

check.q: Tap to see: what is the key rule that turns subtraction into addition?
check.answer: a − b = a + (−b) — subtracting an integer is the same as adding its opposite.

levels.miaWin: You've unlocked the biggest shortcut in integer math! 🔑

levels.title: Subtracting a Negative Integer
levels.mia: Here's where the magic really shows — subtracting a NEGATIVE integer actually makes the answer BIGGER!
levels.body:
When subtracting a negative integer, the opposite of a negative is POSITIVE — so the two negative signs together flip into addition. In short: subtracting a negative = adding a positive.

Subtracting −6 flips into adding +6 — the token hops to the RIGHT, not the left
Example: 5 − (−3) becomes 5 + (3) = 8. Subtracting −3 actually INCREASED the value, because we're adding the opposite of −3, which is +3.
💡 Tip: Think of it like double negation in English — saying 'I do NOT have NO money' actually means you DO have money! Two negatives flip to a positive, in both language and math.

check.q: What is 4 − (−6)?
check.explain: 4 − (−6) = 4 + 6 = 10. Subtracting a negative becomes adding a positive.

levels.miaWin: Subtracting negatives no longer confuses you — you've cracked the code! 🎯

levels.title: Practicing the Subtraction Rule
levels.mia: Let's put it all together with a clear 3-step method you can use for ANY subtraction of integers, every single time!
levels.body:
The 3-step method for a − b: Step 1: Keep the first integer (a) the same. Step 2: Change the subtraction sign to an addition sign. Step 3: Change the SECOND integer (b) to its opposite. Then just add normally!

Three simple steps turn ANY subtraction of integers into an addition you already know how to solve
Example: (−7) − (−2): Step 1: keep −7. Step 2: change − to +. Step 3: change −2 to +2. Now solve: (−7) + 2 = −5.

check.q: What is (−9) − 4?
check.explain: (−9) − 4 becomes (−9) + (−4) = −13 (change the sign to addition, and 4 becomes −4).

levels.miaWin: You've mastered subtraction of integers with a foolproof 3-step method! 🏆

levels.title: Greater Than and Less Than
levels.mia: Let's bring everything together — using the number line to instantly tell whether one integer is greater or less than another!
levels.body:
The symbol > means 'greater than' and < means 'less than'. On a number line, an integer further RIGHT is always greater. So 5 > 2 (5 is to the right of 2), and −8 < −1 (−8 is to the left of −1).

Reading left to right always gives the correct increasing order
Example: Comparing −3 and 4: since 4 is to the right, 4 > −3 (or equivalently, −3 < 4).

check.q: Tap to see: what does the symbol < mean, and how can you remember it?
check.answer: < means "less than" — the smaller (open) side of the symbol faces the bigger number, like a hungry mouth opening toward the larger value.

levels.miaWin: You can now compare any two integers with confidence! ⚖️

levels.title: Ordering Several Integers
levels.mia: Now let's level up — putting a WHOLE group of integers in order, from smallest to largest!
levels.body:
To order several integers: imagine (or draw) a number line, and arrange them exactly as they would appear from LEFT (smallest) to RIGHT (largest). Remember — ALL negative integers are smaller than ALL positive integers, and zero sits in between.

Reading the dots left to right gives the correct order, smallest to largest
💡 Tip: When ordering negative integers among themselves, the one with the BIGGEST digit (ignoring sign) is actually the SMALLEST! For example, among −2, −9, −5: the order from smallest to largest is −9, −5, −2.
Example: Order these from smallest to largest: 3, −7, 0, −2, 5. Answer: −7, −2, 0, 3, 5.

check.q: Which of these is correctly ordered from SMALLEST to LARGEST?
check.explain: −8, −3, 2, 5 is correctly ordered from smallest (leftmost) to largest (rightmost) on a number line.

levels.miaWin: You can now order any group of integers like a pro! 📊

levels.title: Ascending and Descending Order
levels.mia: Math has special names for the two directions of ordering — let's learn the proper vocabulary!
levels.body:
Ascending order means arranging numbers from SMALLEST to LARGEST (like climbing UP steps). Descending order means arranging numbers from LARGEST to SMALLEST (like walking DOWN steps).

Same four integers, two directions — ascending climbs up from −4 to 6, descending steps down from 6 to −4
Example: Ascending order of −4, 6, −1, 0: −4, −1, 0, 6. Descending order of the SAME numbers: 6, 0, −1, −4.

check.q: Fill in the blank: Arranging numbers from largest to smallest is called ____ order.
check.answer: descending
check.explain: Descending order means arranging numbers from largest to smallest, like walking down steps.

levels.miaWin: Ascending, descending — you've completely mastered ordering integers! 🏆

levels.title: Putting It All Together
levels.mia: You've learned 5 separate integer skills — now let's combine them to solve a real multi-step problem, just like a true math detective!
levels.body:
Real problems rarely use just ONE integer skill at a time. A single question might ask you to represent a situation as an integer, plot it, then add or subtract to find a final answer. The trick is to break the problem into small steps and tackle them one at a time.

Most word problems are really just these 3 steps chained together
Example: A lift is at the 2nd floor (+2). It goes down 5 floors, then up 1 floor. Step 1 (represent): start at +2. Step 2 (subtract): 2 + (−5) = −3. Step 3 (add): (−3) + 1 = −2. The lift ends at the 2nd basement floor (−2).

check.q: Tap to see: what is the best FIRST step when solving a multi-part integer word problem?
check.answer: Represent the starting situation as an integer first — then handle each change (add or subtract) one step at a time, in order.

levels.miaWin: You can now break down ANY multi-step integer problem into simple parts! 🧩

levels.title: Choosing the Right Operation
levels.mia: The trickiest part of word problems is deciding WHICH integer rule to use. Let's learn to spot the clues!
levels.body:
Certain words are clues for which integer operation to use: 'gain', 'rises', 'profit', 'above' usually mean ADD a positive. 'Loses', 'drops', 'loss', 'below' usually mean ADD a negative (or subtract). 'How much more/less' or 'difference' usually means SUBTRACT. 'Which is bigger/smaller' means COMPARE on the number line.

💡 Tip: Always identify the ZERO point first (ground level, sea level, starting score) — every other number in the problem is an integer measured from THAT zero.
Example: 'Town A is at −5m elevation and Town B is at 3m elevation. What is the difference in their elevations?' This needs SUBTRACTION: 3 − (−5) = 3 + 5 = 8m.

check.q: A question asks "how much warmer is +4°C than −9°C?" Which operation should you use?
check.explain: “How much warmer/more” means finding a DIFFERENCE, which uses subtraction: 4 − (−9) = 4 + 9 = 13°C warmer.

levels.miaWin: You can now spot exactly which integer rule a word problem needs! 🔍

levels.title: Challenge: The Full Journey
levels.mia: Time for the ultimate integer challenge — a multi-stage journey using EVERY skill from this chapter!
levels.body:
Let's solve one big problem using everything: representing, plotting, ordering, adding, and subtracting integers — all in one go.

Problem: A scuba diver starts at the surface (0m). She dives down 12m, rises 4m to look at a fish, then dives down another 9m to reach the seabed. (a) Represent each stage as an integer. (b) Find her final depth. (c) Is she deeper than a diver at −15m?

Solution: (a) Stage 1: −12, Stage 2: +4, Stage 3: −9. (b) Final depth: 0 + (−12) + 4 + (−9) = (−12−9) + 4 = (−21) + 4 = −17m. (c) Compare −17 and −15: since −17 is further left (smaller), our diver at −17m IS deeper than the diver at −15m.

check.q: A hot air balloon starts at 0m, rises 600m, descends 850m, then rises 120m. What is its final height (as an integer)?

levels.miaWin: Incredible! You've just solved a complete real-world integer challenge using every skill in this chapter! 🏅

levels.title: What is a Fraction?
levels.mia: Hi! I'm Mia 🦊 Ever shared a chocolate bar with a friend? Then you've already used fractions! Let's find out what they really mean.
levels.body:
A fraction is a number that represents a part of a whole. When we divide something into equal parts, each part is a fraction of the whole thing.

One out of two equal parts is written as the fraction 1/2
Example: If a pizza is cut into 4 equal slices and you eat 1 slice, you ate 1/4 (one-fourth) of the pizza.

check.q: Tap to think: if you cut an apple into 2 equal pieces and eat 1 piece, what fraction did you eat?
check.answer: You ate 1/2 (one-half) of the apple — 1 piece out of the 2 equal pieces.

levels.miaWin: Yes! You're already thinking in fractions! 🎉

levels.title: Numerator & Denominator
levels.mia: Every fraction has two special parts with their own names — let's meet the numerator and the denominator!
levels.body:
A fraction is written as numerator / denominator. The denominator (bottom number) tells us how many equal parts the whole is divided into. The numerator (top number) tells us how many of those parts we are talking about.

3/5 — numerator 3 (shaded), denominator 5 (total parts)
💡 Tip: Denominator is at the bottom, like the ground — it tells the TOTAL number of equal parts.

check.q: Tap to check: in the fraction 4/7, which number is the denominator?
check.answer: 7 is the denominator — it shows the whole is divided into 7 equal parts. 4 is the numerator.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! Numerator on top, denominator on the bottom — got it! ⭐

levels.title: Fraction of a Collection
levels.mia: Fractions don't only work on single objects — they also work on a GROUP of things, like a bunch of marbles or a basket of fruits!
levels.body:
A fraction can also represent a part of a collection (a group of objects), not just a part of one single shape.

Fractions can describe part of a group, not just part of one shape
Example: In a class of 30 students, if 18 are girls, then 18/30 of the class are girls.

check.q: Tap to try: A box has 10 pencils. 3 are red. What fraction of the pencils are red?
check.answer: 3/10 of the pencils are red — 3 out of the 10 total pencils.

levels.miaWin: Excellent! You can now spot fractions in groups too! 🚀

levels.title: Proper Fractions
levels.mia: Welcome back! Now let's sort fractions into families. First up — proper fractions!
levels.body:
A proper fraction is a fraction where the numerator is smaller than the denominator. This means the fraction represents a value less than 1 whole.

3/4 fills less than the whole rectangle — a proper fraction
Examples of proper fractions: 1/2, 3/5, 7/9, 2/3 — in each, the top number is smaller than the bottom number.

check.q: Tap to check: is 5/8 a proper fraction?
check.answer: Yes! 5 is smaller than 8, so 5/8 is a proper fraction — it represents less than 1 whole.

levels.miaWin: Great! Numerator smaller than denominator = proper fraction. 🎉

levels.title: Improper Fractions
levels.mia: Now here's a twist — what happens when the top number is BIGGER than the bottom number? Let's find out!
levels.body:
An improper fraction is a fraction where the numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator. This means the fraction represents a value equal to or greater than 1 whole.

7/3 needs more than 2 whole rectangles to show all 7 parts
Examples of improper fractions: 5/4, 9/7, 11/11, 8/3 — in each, the numerator is greater than or equal to the denominator.

check.q: Tap to check: is 9/4 a proper or improper fraction?
check.answer: 9/4 is an improper fraction, because 9 (numerator) is greater than 4 (denominator) — it represents more than 1 whole.

levels.miaWin: Exactly! Bigger top number means improper. ⭐

levels.title: Mixed Fractions
levels.mia: Improper fractions can also be written in a friendlier way — as a whole number plus a smaller fraction. Meet the mixed fraction!
levels.body:
A mixed fraction combines a whole number with a proper fraction. Every improper fraction can be converted to a mixed fraction, and vice versa.

Divide numerator by denominator: quotient = whole number, remainder/divisor = the fraction part
💡 Tip: To go back from a mixed fraction to improper: multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and keep the same denominator.

check.q: Tap to try: convert the improper fraction 11/4 into a mixed fraction.
check.answer: 11 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 3, so 11/4 = 2 3/4 (two and three-fourths).

levels.miaWin: Wonderful! You can flip between improper and mixed fractions now! 🚀

levels.title: Marking Fractions Between 0 and 1
levels.mia: Hi! I'm Mia 🦊 We've placed whole numbers on a number line before — now let's place FRACTIONS on it too!
levels.body:
To mark a fraction like 3/4 on a number line, divide the space between 0 and 1 into the number of parts shown by the denominator. Then count that many parts from 0, shown by the numerator.

The gap from 0 to 1 is divided into equal parts matching the denominator
Example: To mark 3/5, split the segment from 0 to 1 into 5 equal parts, then go to the 3rd mark from 0.

check.q: Tap to think: to mark 1/4 on a number line, into how many equal parts should you split the gap from 0 to 1?
