check.answer: Into 4 equal parts (matching the denominator), then mark the 1st point from 0.

levels.miaWin: Yes! You're now placing fractions on the number line like a pro! 🎉

levels.title: Fractions Beyond 1
levels.mia: What about fractions bigger than 1, like 7/4? No problem — the number line just keeps going past 1, 2, 3...
levels.body:
For fractions greater than 1 (improper fractions), the number line continues past 1 into 2, 3, and so on. Each whole number gap is still divided into the same number of equal parts (matching the denominator).

7/4 = 1 3/4, which lies between the whole numbers 1 and 2
💡 Tip: Convert an improper fraction to a mixed fraction first — the whole number part tells you WHICH segment to look in!

check.q: Tap to try: between which two whole numbers does 9/4 lie on the number line?
check.answer: 9/4 = 2 1/4, so it lies between the whole numbers 2 and 3.

levels.miaWin: Great! Fractions bigger than 1 just live further along the line. ⭐

levels.title: Comparing Fraction Positions
levels.mia: Here's something powerful — once fractions are placed on a number line, comparing them becomes as easy as looking at WHO is further right!
levels.body:
On a number line, a fraction that is further to the right is always greater than one that is further to the left. This gives us a visual way to compare and order fractions.

Whichever fraction sits further right on the line is the greater fraction
Example: Since 2/5 is to the left of 4/5 on the number line, we know 2/5 < 4/5.

check.q: Tap to try: on a number line, 5/6 is to the right of 1/6. What does that tell you?
check.answer: It tells you that 5/6 is greater than 1/6, since fractions further right on the number line are always bigger.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! The number line turns comparing fractions into a visual breeze! 🚀

levels.title: What Are Equivalent Fractions?
levels.mia: Did you know two fractions that LOOK different can actually mean the exact same amount? Let's see this magic trick!
levels.body:
Equivalent fractions are different fractions that represent the same value or the same part of a whole.

Same shaded area, different number of pieces — equivalent fractions
Example: 1/3, 2/6, and 3/9 are all equivalent fractions — they all represent the same amount.

check.q: Tap to think: do 1/2 and 2/4 represent the same amount?
check.answer: Yes! 1/2 and 2/4 are equivalent fractions — both represent exactly half of a whole.

levels.miaWin: Yes! Same value, different look — that's the magic of equivalent fractions! 🎉

levels.title: Making Equivalent Fractions
levels.mia: Here's the secret rule to MAKE equivalent fractions yourself — multiply (or divide) both top and bottom by the SAME number!
levels.body:
To find an equivalent fraction, multiply (or divide) both the numerator and denominator by the same non-zero number. This keeps the value of the fraction unchanged.

Multiply numerator and denominator by the same number to get an equivalent fraction
💡 Tip: You can also DIVIDE both numbers by the same factor to get a simpler equivalent fraction — like turning 6/9 back into 2/3!

check.q: Tap to try: find an equivalent fraction of 3/4 by multiplying top and bottom by 2.
check.answer: 3/4 × (2/2) = 6/8. So 3/4 and 6/8 are equivalent fractions.

levels.miaWin: Perfect! Same trick works every time — multiply both by the same number! ⭐

levels.title: Simplest Form of a Fraction
levels.mia: Sometimes a fraction can be made smaller and simpler while still meaning the same thing. That's called reducing to the simplest form!
levels.body:
A fraction is in its simplest form (or lowest form) when the numerator and denominator have no common factor other than 1. To simplify, divide both numbers by their Highest Common Factor (HCF).

Dividing by the HCF gives the simplest form of a fraction
Example: 2/3 is already in simplest form because 2 and 3 share no common factor except 1.

check.q: Tap to try: simplify the fraction 8/12 to its lowest form.
check.answer: HCF of 8 and 12 is 4. Dividing both by 4: 8÷4=2, 12÷4=3. So 8/12 simplifies to 2/3.

levels.miaWin: Awesome! You're a fraction-simplifying champion now! 🚀

levels.title: Comparing Like Fractions
levels.mia: Fractions with the SAME denominator are called 'like fractions' — and comparing them is super easy!
levels.body:
Like fractions have the same denominator. To compare like fractions, just compare the numerators — the bigger numerator means the bigger fraction.

With the same denominator, the bigger numerator wins
Example: Comparing 3/7 and 5/7 — both have denominator 7, so we compare 3 and 5. Since 5 > 3, we get 5/7 > 3/7.

check.q: Tap to try: which is bigger, 6/9 or 4/9?
check.answer: 6/9 is bigger, because both have the same denominator (9), and 6 > 4.

levels.miaWin: Nice and easy! Same bottom number, just compare the tops. 🎉

levels.title: Comparing Unlike Fractions
levels.mia: What if the denominators are DIFFERENT? Don't worry — we just need one extra step before comparing!
levels.body:
Unlike fractions have different denominators. To compare them, first convert them into like fractions using their LCM as the common denominator, then compare the numerators.

Convert unlike fractions to a common denominator before comparing
💡 Tip: A quick trick for two fractions: cross-multiply! For a/b vs c/d, compare a×d with b×c.

check.q: Tap to try: which is bigger, 1/2 or 2/5?

levels.miaWin: Great work! You can now compare ANY two fractions! ⭐

levels.title: Ordering Fractions
levels.mia: Now let's level up — arranging THREE OR MORE fractions in order from smallest to biggest, or biggest to smallest!
levels.body:
To order several fractions, convert all of them to like fractions using the LCM of all denominators as the common denominator. Then arrange the numerators in the required order.

Convert all fractions to a common denominator, then compare numerators
Example: To order 3/4, 1/2, 2/3 — use LCM 12: 3/4=9/12, 1/2=6/12, 2/3=8/12. So 1/2 < 2/3 < 3/4.

check.q: Tap to try: arrange 1/4, 1/2, 3/8 from smallest to largest.

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You can now order any set of fractions like a pro! 🚀

levels.title: Finding a Fraction of a Number
levels.mia: Hi! I'm Mia 🦊 Ever wondered how to find '1/4 of 20 toffees'? Let's learn the simple trick!
levels.body:
To find a fraction of a quantity, divide the quantity by the denominator, then multiply the result by the numerator.

Divide by the denominator first, then multiply by the numerator
Example: 1/2 of 16 = 16÷2 = 8. 2/3 of 9 = (9÷3)×2 = 3×2 = 6.

check.q: Tap to try: what is 1/5 of 30?

levels.miaWin: Yes! Divide then multiply — that's the whole trick! 🎉

levels.title: Visualising Fraction of a Quantity
levels.mia: Let's SEE this idea in action with a real group of objects — it makes the trick click even faster!
levels.body:
Splitting a group into equal smaller groups (matching the denominator) and counting how many groups we need (matching the numerator) shows exactly why dividing then multiplying works.

Split into 3 equal groups (denominator), then take 2 of those groups (numerator)
💡 Tip: The quantity MUST divide evenly by the denominator for whole-number groups — this works perfectly when numbers are chosen carefully!

check.q: Tap to try: what is 3/5 of 25?
check.answer: 25 ÷ 5 = 5 per group, then 5 × 3 = 15. So 3/5 of 25 is 15.

levels.miaWin: Wonderful! Now you can SEE why the trick works! ⭐

levels.title: Fraction of a Quantity in Real Life
levels.mia: This skill is everywhere in daily life — discounts, recipes, scores, and more! Let's apply it to real situations.
levels.body:
Finding a fraction of a quantity helps solve everyday problems: finding part of a distance travelled, part of a class with a certain trait, part of money saved, and much more.

The same divide-then-multiply method solves real-world fraction problems
Example: A shop offers 1/4 off a ₹800 item. The discount is 800÷4 = ₹200, so the new price is 800−200 = ₹600.

check.q: Tap to try: a recipe needs 2/5 of 30 grams of sugar. How many grams is that?
check.answer: 30 ÷ 5 = 6, then 6 × 2 = 12. So 2/5 of 30 grams is 12 grams.

levels.miaWin: Amazing! You can now use fractions to solve real-world problems with confidence! 🚀

levels.title: Adding Like Fractions
levels.mia: Time to add fractions! Good news — adding fractions with the SAME denominator is wonderfully simple.
levels.body:
To add like fractions (same denominator), simply add the numerators and keep the denominator the same.

Add numerators (1+2=3), keep the denominator (4)
Example: 3/8 + 2/8 = (3+2)/8 = 5/8. Same denominator, just add the top numbers.

check.q: Tap to try: what is 2/9 + 4/9?
check.answer: 2/9 + 4/9 = (2+4)/9 = 6/9 (which can be simplified to 2/3).

levels.miaWin: Easy peasy! Add the tops, keep the bottom. 🎉

levels.title: Subtracting Like Fractions
levels.mia: Subtraction follows the exact same idea as addition — just subtract instead!
levels.body:
To subtract like fractions (same denominator), subtract the numerators and keep the denominator the same.

Subtract numerators (4−1=3), keep the denominator (5)
Example: 7/10 − 3/10 = (7−3)/10 = 4/10 = 2/5 (after simplifying).

check.q: Tap to try: what is 5/6 minus 2/6?
check.answer: 5/6 − 2/6 = (5−2)/6 = 3/6, which simplifies to 1/2.

levels.miaWin: Wonderful! Same denominator means same easy rule. ⭐

levels.title: Adding & Subtracting Unlike Fractions
levels.mia: Last challenge — what about fractions with DIFFERENT denominators? We use the same trick from comparing fractions!
levels.body:
For unlike fractions (different denominators), first find the LCM of the denominators, convert both fractions to equivalent like fractions, then add or subtract the numerators.

Convert to a common denominator first, then add or subtract as usual
💡 Tip: For mixed fractions, first convert each to an improper fraction, then follow the same steps before converting back if needed.

check.q: Tap to try: what is 2/3 minus 1/6?

levels.miaWin: Incredible! You've mastered adding and subtracting ALL kinds of fractions! 🚀

levels.title: Spotting the Right Operation
levels.mia: Hi! I'm Mia 🦊 Word problems mix EVERYTHING we've learned about fractions. The first skill is figuring out WHICH operation to use!
levels.body:
Look for clue words: 'altogether' or 'in total' often means addition. 'Left' or 'remaining' often means subtraction. 'Of' (like '2/3 of the class') usually means finding a fraction of a quantity (multiply).

Clue words in a word problem hint at which operation to use
Example: “Rahul ate 1/4 of a cake, his sister ate 1/4 more. How much did they eat altogether?” — “altogether” signals addition: 1/4 + 1/4.

check.q: Tap to think: in the sentence “A tank is 3/4 full; how much is NOT filled?”, which operation should you use?
check.answer: Subtraction — you would calculate 1 − 3/4 to find the unfilled fraction.

levels.miaWin: Great instinct! Spotting clue words is half the battle in word problems! 🎉

levels.title: Multi-Step Fraction Problems
levels.mia: Some problems need MORE than one step. Let's break a tricky one down piece by piece!
levels.body:
For multi-step problems, solve one step at a time: first find what the problem is really asking, do the first operation, then use that answer to do the next operation.

Break the problem into small steps, using each answer in the next step
💡 Tip: After EVERY step, ask: “What does this number represent?” It helps avoid using the wrong amount in the next step.

check.q: Tap to try: a 30-litre tank loses 1/5 of its water, then 1/3 of what remains is used. How much water is left after BOTH losses?
check.answer: 1/5 of 30 = 6 litres lost, leaving 24 litres. Then 1/3 of 24 = 8 litres used, leaving 24−8 = 16 litres.

levels.miaWin: Excellent! Breaking it into steps makes even tricky problems manageable! ⭐

levels.title: Challenge: The Full Fractions Journey
levels.mia: Time for the ultimate fractions challenge — a problem using EVERY skill from this whole chapter, all in one go!
levels.body:
Let's solve one big problem using everything: identifying fraction types, simplifying, comparing, finding a fraction of a quantity, and adding/subtracting — all together.

Problem: Meera has ₹600. She spends 1/4 of it on books and 1/3 of it on stationery. (a) How much does she spend on books? (b) How much on stationery? (c) What fraction of her money is left, and how much is that in rupees?

Solution: (a) 1/4 of 600 = 600÷4 = ₹150 on books. (b) 1/3 of 600 = 600÷3 = ₹200 on stationery. (c) Total spent: 150+200 = ₹350. Fraction spent: 350/600, which simplifies to 7/12. So fraction left = 1 − 7/12 = 5/12, which is (5/12)×600 = ₹250.

check.q: A 36-page book has 1/4 of its pages read on day 1, then 1/3 of the REMAINING pages read on day 2. How many pages are left unread after day 2?
check.explain: Day 1: 1/4 of 36 = 9 pages read, leaving 27 pages. Day 2: 1/3 of 27 = 9 pages read, leaving 27−9 = 18 pages unread.

levels.miaWin: Incredible! You've just solved a complete real-world fractions challenge using every skill in this chapter! 🏅

levels.title: What Is a Decimal?
levels.mia: Hi! I'm Mia 🦊 Ever seen a price tag like ₹45.50? That little dot is called a decimal point — and today we're going to crack its secret code!
levels.body:
A decimal number is a way of writing numbers that are not whole — numbers that fall between two whole numbers. It uses a decimal point (.) to separate the whole number part from the fractional part.

In the number 3.7, the part before the dot (3) is the whole number part, and the part after the dot (7) is the decimal part — it tells us 'a bit more than 3'.

Example: 12.5 means 12 whole units, plus a little bit more (0.5, or half a unit).

check.q: Tap to think: in the decimal 8.3, what does the 8 represent?
check.answer: The 8 is the whole number part — it means 8 whole units, plus a bit extra shown by the .3.

levels.miaWin: Yes! You've cracked the decimal code! 🎉

levels.title: Place Value in Decimals
levels.mia: Whole numbers have a ones place, tens place... decimals have special places too, but they go the OTHER way after the dot!
levels.body:
Just like whole numbers have place values (ones, tens, hundreds), the digits after the decimal point have their own place values too — but they get smaller as you move right.

The first digit after the decimal point is in the tenths place. The second digit after the decimal point is in the hundredths place.

💡 Tip: After the decimal point, place values are tenths, hundredths, thousandths — each one TEN TIMES SMALLER than the one before, just like ones, tens, hundreds grow ten times bigger before the dot.

check.q: Tap to try: in the number 9.42, which digit is in the hundredths place?
check.answer: The digit 2 is in the hundredths place — it is the second digit after the decimal point.

levels.miaWin: Brilliant! You can now read a decimal place value chart like a pro! 🚀

levels.title: Tenths (1/10 = 0.1)
levels.mia: Let's zoom into the FIRST decimal place — the tenths! Imagine slicing one whole into 10 equal strips.
levels.body:
When a whole is divided into 10 equal parts, each part is called a tenth. As a fraction, one part is 1/10. As a decimal, it's written as 0.1.

Example: 7/10 of a chocolate bar = 0.7 of the bar. 1/10 = 0.1, 5/10 = 0.5, 9/10 = 0.9.

check.q: Tap to try: a strip of 10 boxes has 6 shaded. Write this as a decimal.
check.answer: 6 shaded out of 10 is 6/10, which is written as the decimal 0.6.

levels.miaWin: Yes! Tenths are simply 'out of 10' written with a dot! ⭐

levels.title: Hundredths (1/100 = 0.01)
levels.mia: Now let's slice even thinner — what if we cut the whole into 100 tiny equal squares?
levels.body:
When a whole is divided into 100 equal parts, each part is called a hundredth. As a fraction, one part is 1/100. As a decimal, it's written as 0.01.

Example: 45/100 = 0.45, 3/100 = 0.03 (notice the extra zero needed to hold the tenths place!).

check.q: Tap to try: 8 out of 100 squares are shaded. Write this as a decimal.
check.answer: 8/100 is written as 0.08 — a zero is needed in the tenths place since there are no full tenths.

levels.miaWin: Excellent! You can now picture hundredths as a 10x10 grid! 🎉

levels.title: Writing & Representing Decimals
levels.mia: Decimals can be written in many forms — as fractions, in words, in figures, on grids, or on a number line. Let's connect them all!
levels.body:
A decimal can come from a fraction with denominator 10, 100, etc. We can write the SAME value as a fraction, in figures, and in words.

Example: 3/10 → figure: 0.3 → words: 'zero point three'. And 25/100 → figure: 0.25 → words: 'zero point two five' (each digit after the dot is read separately, not as 'twenty-five').

Decimals can also be shown on a number line — the space between two whole numbers is split into 10 equal tenths.

0.6 sits between 0 and 1 — six tenths of the way across

check.q: Tap to try: write 9/100 in figures and read it in words.
check.answer: 9/100 is written as 0.09, read as 'zero point zero nine' (each digit after the dot read separately).

levels.miaWin: Wonderful! You can now switch between fractions, figures, words, and number lines! 🚀

levels.title: Equivalent Decimals
levels.mia: Here's a fun decimal trick — adding zeros at the END of a decimal doesn't change its value at all!
levels.body:
Equivalent decimals are decimals that look different but represent the same value. You can add (or remove) zeros at the END of the decimal part without changing its value.

Example: 0.5 = 0.50 = 0.500 — all mean 'five tenths'. Think of it as 5/10 = 50/100 = 500/1000.
💡 Tip: A zero added BEFORE the whole number part or in the MIDDLE of digits does change the value — only trailing zeros (at the very end) are 'free' to add or remove.

check.q: Tap to think: are 2.3 and 2.30 the same value?
check.answer: Yes! 2.3 and 2.30 are equivalent decimals — the extra zero at the end does not change the value.

levels.miaWin: Yes! Trailing zeros are just decoration — the value stays the same! 🎉

levels.title: Converting Fractions ↔ Decimals
levels.mia: Decimals and fractions are really just two outfits for the same number. Let's learn to switch between them!
levels.body:
To convert a fraction to a decimal when the denominator is 10, 100, or 1000, simply place the decimal point so that the number of digits after it matches the number of zeros in the denominator.

Example: 7/10 = 0.7 (1 digit after the dot, matching the 1 zero). 23/100 = 0.23 (2 digits after the dot, matching the 2 zeros).

To convert a decimal to a fraction, write the digits after the decimal point as the numerator, and use 10, 100, or 1000 (matching the number of decimal digits) as the denominator.

check.q: Tap to try: convert 0.6 to a fraction.
check.answer: 0.6 has 1 digit after the dot, so it becomes 6/10 (which simplifies to 3/5).

levels.miaWin: Great! You can now flip between fractions and decimals with ease! 🚀

levels.title: Comparing Decimals
levels.mia: Comparing decimals is just like comparing whole numbers — but you compare place by place, starting from the LEFT!
levels.body:
To compare decimals, first compare the whole number parts. If they're equal, compare the tenths digit, then the hundredths digit, and so on — moving left to right.

Example: Compare 4.6 and 4.58. Whole parts are equal (4=4). Tenths: 6 vs 5 → 6 is bigger, so 4.6 > 4.58, even though 4.58 has more digits!
💡 Tip: To compare easily, give decimals the SAME number of decimal digits by adding trailing zeros first — e.g. compare 4.60 with 4.58.

check.q: Tap to try: which is bigger, 3.45 or 3.5?
check.answer: 3.5 is bigger. Writing 3.5 as 3.50, compare tenths: 5 > 4, so 3.5 > 3.45.

levels.miaWin: Yes! Left to right, place by place — comparing decimals is easy now! ⭐

levels.title: Ordering Decimals
levels.mia: Now let's level up — arranging a whole GROUP of decimals from smallest to biggest, or biggest to smallest!
levels.body:
To order decimals, give every number the SAME number of decimal places (by adding trailing zeros), then compare them place by place, just like before.

Example: Order 2.5, 2.05, 2.55 from smallest to largest. Rewrite as 2.50, 2.05, 2.55. Comparing: 2.05 < 2.50 < 2.55. So the order is 2.05, 2.5, 2.55.

check.q: Tap to try: order 0.8, 0.08, 0.18 from smallest to largest.
check.answer: Rewrite as 0.80, 0.08, 0.18 — comparing: 0.08 < 0.18 < 0.80. So the order is 0.08, 0.18, 0.8.

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You can now order any set of decimals like a pro! 🚀

levels.title: Decimals in Money (Rupees & Paise)
levels.mia: Every time you see a price tag, you're reading a decimal! Let's see how rupees and paise use decimals.
levels.body:
In Indian money, 100 paise = 1 rupee. So paise are written as the decimal part of a rupee amount — just like hundredths!

Example: ₹25 and 40 paise is written as ₹25.40. Here, 40 paise = 40/100 of a rupee = 0.40 rupees.
💡 Tip: When writing money in decimal form, ALWAYS use exactly 2 digits after the point — ₹8.50, not ₹8.5 — since there are 100 paise in a rupee.

check.q: Tap to try: write ₹7 and 5 paise using a decimal.
check.answer: 5 paise = 5/100 rupees = 0.05 rupees, so ₹7 and 5 paise is written as ₹7.05.

levels.miaWin: Yes! Now you can read any price tag like a decimal expert! 🎉

levels.title: Decimals in Length & Measurement
levels.mia: Decimals also help us measure things precisely — like the length of your pencil, or the distance to school!
levels.body:
Common length units relate by powers of 10, just like decimal place values: 10 mm = 1 cm, and 100 cm = 1 m. So measurements smaller than a unit are written using decimals.

Example: A pencil that is 14 cm and 5 mm long is 14.5 cm (since 5 mm = 5/10 cm = 0.5 cm). A wall that is 3 m and 25 cm tall is 3.25 m (since 25 cm = 25/100 m = 0.25 m).

check.q: Tap to try: write 8 m and 60 cm using a decimal (in metres).
check.answer: 60 cm = 60/100 m = 0.60 m, so 8 m and 60 cm is written as 8.60 m or 8.6 m.

levels.miaWin: Wonderful! Decimals make precise measuring so much easier! 🚀

levels.title: Adding Decimals
levels.mia: Adding decimals is just like adding whole numbers — the secret is lining up the decimal points first!
levels.body:
To add decimals: write the numbers one below the other so that the decimal points line up. Add extra zeros if needed so both numbers have the same number of decimal digits, then add as usual, keeping the decimal point in the same place in the answer.

💡 Tip: Always make BOTH numbers have the same number of decimal digits (using trailing zeros) before lining them up — it avoids mistakes when adding column by column.

check.q: Tap to try: what is 3.2 + 1.45? (Hint: write 3.2 as 3.20 first)

levels.miaWin: Yes! Line up those decimal points and adding becomes easy! 🎉

levels.title: Subtracting Decimals
levels.mia: Subtracting decimals follows the SAME golden rule — line up those decimal points before you start!
levels.body:
To subtract decimals: line up the decimal points, fill in any missing decimal digits with zeros, then subtract column by column just like whole numbers, borrowing when needed.

Example: A 5 m ribbon is cut to 2.35 m. Ribbon left = 5.00 − 2.35 = 2.65 m.

check.q: Tap to try: what is 6.4 − 2.75? (Hint: write 6.4 as 6.40 first)

levels.miaWin: Great! You've now mastered both adding and subtracting decimals! 🚀

levels.title: Word Problems with Decimals
levels.mia: Time to put EVERYTHING together — using decimals to solve real-life problems involving money, length, and more!
levels.body:
Decimal word problems usually involve money, length, weight, or quantities. The key is to spot the right operation: words like 'total' or 'altogether' usually mean add, while 'left', 'remaining', or 'difference' usually mean subtract.

Example: Riya buys a notebook for ₹35.50 and a pen for ₹12.75. Total cost = 35.50 + 12.75 = ₹48.25. If she pays with a ₹50 note, change = 50.00 − 48.25 = ₹1.75.
💡 Tip: Always write money and measurement answers with the correct number of decimal places (2 for rupees-paise, matching the unit for measurements) so your final answer makes real-world sense.

check.q: Tap to try: a jug holds 1.5 litres of juice. If 0.65 litres is poured out, how much juice is left?
check.answer: 1.50 − 0.65 = 0.85 litres of juice is left.

levels.miaWin: Incredible! You've completed the entire Decimals chapter — money, length, and word problems mastered! 🏅

levels.title: Place Value Chart for Decimals
levels.mia: Every digit in a decimal has its own special job to do — let's build a place value chart and see exactly where each digit lives!
levels.body:
Just like whole numbers have a place value chart (hundreds, tens, ones), decimals extend that same chart to the right of the decimal point: tenths, hundredths, thousandths — each one ten times smaller than the one before.

💡 Tip: The THIRD digit after the decimal point is always the thousandths place — it is 1/1000 of a whole, one thousand times smaller than the ones place.

check.q: Tap to try: in 245.678, which digit is in the thousandths place, and what is it worth?
check.answer: 8 is in the thousandths place — it is worth 8 thousandths, or 8/1000 of a whole.

levels.miaWin: Yes! You've mapped out the entire decimal place value chart! 🎉

levels.title: Writing Decimals in Expanded Form
levels.mia: Expanded form breaks a decimal apart into what each digit is REALLY worth, then adds them all back up!
levels.body:
To write a decimal in expanded form, write it as the sum of the value of each digit — whole number places PLUS decimal places.

Example: 32.46 = 30 + 2 + 0.4 + 0.06 — the digit 4 is worth 0.4 (4 tenths) and the digit 6 is worth 0.06 (6 hundredths).

check.q: Tap to try: write 32.46 in expanded form.

levels.miaWin: Amazing! You can now break any decimal down into its true place values! 🚀

levels.title: Plotting Decimals in Tenths
levels.mia: A number line isn't just for whole numbers — decimals live in the spaces BETWEEN them too! Let's zoom into the gap between 0 and 1.
levels.body:
The space between any two whole numbers can be split into 10 equal tenths. Each little step to the right adds 0.1.

💡 Tip: Count the small steps from 0 — each step is one tenth (0.1), so 6 steps from 0 lands you exactly on 0.6.

check.q: Tap to try: on a number line from 3 to 4 split into tenths, where would 3.4 sit?
check.answer: 3.4 sits four small steps (four-tenths) past 3, closer to the 3 end than the 4 end.

levels.miaWin: Great! You can now place any tenths decimal on a number line! ⭐

levels.title: Zooming in with Hundredths
levels.mia: Let's zoom in even closer! Between two tenths marks, there's room for 10 tiny hundredth steps.
levels.body:
To plot a decimal like 0.64 precisely, zoom into the space between 0.6 and 0.7 and split THAT into 10 equal hundredths.

Example: 0.25 sits exactly halfway between 0.2 and 0.3 — that's 5 hundredth-steps past 0.2.

check.q: Tap to try: between 0.2 and 0.3 on a hundredths number line, where would 0.25 sit?
check.answer: 0.25 sits exactly halfway between 0.2 and 0.3 — 5 hundredth-steps past 0.2.

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! Zooming in on number lines helps you picture decimals precisely! 🚀

levels.title: Fraction to Decimal
levels.mia: Fractions and decimals are two outfits for the same number. Let's learn to turn any fraction with a 10, 100, or 1000 denominator into a decimal!
levels.body:
When the denominator is 10, 100, or 1000, converting to a decimal is simple: count the zeros in the denominator — that tells you how many digits go after the decimal point.

💡 Tip: If the numerator has fewer digits than the number of zeros, fill the gap with leading zeros right after the decimal point — e.g. 7/1000 becomes 0.007, not 0.7.

check.q: Tap to try: convert 7/1000 to a decimal.
check.answer: 0.007 — three decimal digits, because the denominator 1000 has three zeros.

levels.miaWin: Great start! Fractions to decimals is now easy for you! 🎉

levels.title: Decimal to Fraction — and Simplifying
levels.mia: Going the other way is just as simple — and then we simplify the fraction down to its lowest terms!
levels.body:
To convert a decimal to a fraction: write the digits after the decimal point as the numerator, use 10/100/1000 (matching the number of decimal digits) as the denominator, then simplify by dividing both parts by their HCF.

Example: 0.4 = 4/10 = 2/5 (divide both by their HCF, 2).

check.q: Tap to try: convert 0.4 to a fraction in simplest form.
check.answer: 0.4 = 4/10, which simplifies to 2/5 (dividing both by 2).

levels.miaWin: Excellent! You can now flip fluently between fractions and decimals, fully simplified! 🚀

levels.title: Money & Shopping Word Problems
levels.mia: Time to put decimals to work in real life — starting with a trip to the market!
levels.body:
Decimal word problems about money usually ask for a total cost or the change received. Watch for keywords: 'total' or 'altogether' means add; 'change' or 'left over' means subtract.

Example: Aman buys fruits worth ₹64.50 and vegetables worth ₹28.75. Total spent = 64.50 + 28.75 = ₹93.25. If he pays with a ₹100 note, change = 100.00 − 93.25 = ₹6.75.
💡 Tip: Always line up decimal points and use trailing zeros so both amounts have the same number of decimal digits before adding or subtracting money.

check.q: Tap to try: Priya buys a book for ₹85.40 and a pencil box for ₹34.60. What is the total cost?

levels.miaWin: Nice! You're solving real shopping problems with decimals like a pro! 🎉

levels.title: Measurement & Multi-Step Word Problems
levels.mia: Now let's tackle problems with LENGTH, WEIGHT, and multiple steps — breaking each one down piece by piece!
levels.body:
For multi-step decimal problems, solve one step at a time: find what's needed first, use that answer for the next step, and keep units consistent throughout.

Example: A rope is 12.5 m long. A piece of 4.75 m is cut off, then another piece of 2.5 m is cut off. Rope left = 12.50 − 4.75 − 2.50 = 5.25 m.
💡 Tip: In multi-step problems, underline each number and its unit as you read — it helps you decide whether to add or subtract at each step.

check.q: Tap to try: a bag of rice weighs 5.6 kg. 2.35 kg is used one day and 1.4 kg the next day. How much rice is left?
check.answer: 5.60 − 2.35 − 1.40 = 1.85 kg of rice is left.

levels.miaWin: Incredible! You've mastered multi-step decimal word problems! 🏅

levels.title: Quick-Fire Fill in the Blanks
levels.mia: Let's do a rapid recap of everything you've learned about decimals — fill in each blank in your head before checking!
levels.body:
Try these quick recap questions. Think of your answer first, then reveal it below to check yourself.

1. 3/10 written as a decimal is ______.
Answer: 0.3
2. In 5.62, the digit in the hundredths place is ______.
Answer: 2
3. 0.5 and ______ are equivalent decimals (add a trailing zero).
Answer: 0.50
4. 12.7 + 5.46 = ______.
Answer: 18.16
5. 0.75 simplified as a fraction is ______.
Answer: 3/4
💡 Tip: Cover the answer with your hand, say your guess out loud, THEN check — it helps the learning stick much better than just reading!

check.q: Tap to try one more: 8 m and 60 cm written as a decimal (in metres) is ______.

levels.miaWin: Awesome recap! Your decimal fill-in-the-blank skills are sharp! ⭐

levels.title: True or False Challenge
levels.mia: Now let's test your instincts — is each decimal statement TRUE or FALSE? Think fast!
levels.body:
Read each statement, decide TRUE or FALSE, then check your answer.

1. 2.3 and 2.30 represent the same value.
Answer: TRUE — trailing zeros don't change a decimal's value.
2. 0.9 is smaller than 0.19.
Answer: FALSE — comparing tenths first, 9 tenths is much bigger than 1 tenth.
3. The hundredths place is the first digit after the decimal point.
Answer: FALSE — the tenths place comes first; hundredths is second.
4. 100 paise written as a decimal of a rupee is 1.00.
Answer: TRUE — 100 paise = 1 whole rupee.
5. To add decimals, you must line up the decimal points first.
Answer: TRUE — this keeps each digit in its correct place value.
💡 Tip: When in doubt, compare place by place from the LEFT — whole number part first, then tenths, then hundredths.

check.q: Tap to try: TRUE or FALSE — 4.05 is greater than 4.5.
check.answer: FALSE — comparing tenths, 4.5 has 5 tenths while 4.05 has 0 tenths, so 4.5 is greater.

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You've completed the full Decimals practice round-up — great work! 🏅

levels.title: What is Data?
levels.mia: Hi! I'm Mia 🦊 Every day you're surrounded by DATA — your marks, the weather, even how many chocolates are left in the jar. Let's find out what 'data' really means!
levels.body:
Data is a collection of facts, numbers, or observations gathered for a purpose — like the number of students who like different fruits, or the temperature recorded each day for a week.

We collect data so we can study it, understand patterns, and make decisions based on facts instead of guesses.

💡 Tip: If you can COUNT it, MEASURE it, or RECORD it as a fact — it's data!

check.q: Tap to think: is the number of students absent in your class today an example of data? Why?
check.answer: Yes! It is a fact that can be counted and recorded — exactly what makes something data.

levels.miaWin: Yes! You now know what data really means! 🎉

levels.title: Types of Data — Categories & Numbers
levels.mia: Data comes in two flavours — things you can COUNT into categories, and things you can MEASURE as numbers. Let's spot the difference!
levels.body:
Some data groups things into categories (like favourite sport, favourite colour). Other data is numerical — actual measured amounts (like height, marks, temperature).

Example: A class survey of "which pet do you have?" gives category data (Dog, Cat, Fish). A survey of "how many pets do you have?" gives numerical data (0, 1, 2, 3...).

check.q: Tap to try: is "favourite colour" category data or numerical data?
check.answer: Category data — colours like Red, Blue, Green are groups, not measured numbers.

levels.miaWin: Brilliant! You can now tell category data from numerical data! 🚀

levels.title: Collecting Data — Surveys & Observation
levels.mia: Before we can study data, we first need to COLLECT it! Let's learn the two main ways data gets gathered.
levels.body:
Data can be collected by observation (watching and noting things down, like counting cars passing by) or by a survey (asking people questions, like "what is your favourite fruit?").

💡 Tip: The way you collect data should match what you want to find out — watch quietly for counts, or ask questions for opinions.

check.q: Tap to think: to find out how many students walk to school, would you use observation or a survey?
check.answer: Either works! You could observe students arriving, or simply ask (survey) each student how they came to school.

levels.miaWin: Great! You now know how data gets collected in the first place! 🎉

levels.title: Organizing Raw Data into a List
levels.mia: Once we collect data, it's often messy and unordered — that's called RAW DATA. Let's tidy it up!
levels.body:
Raw data is data exactly as it was collected, before being organized. Arranging it into an ordered list (like ascending order, or grouped by category) makes it much easier to study.

Raw data: Marks of 8 students: 7, 9, 6, 9, 8, 7, 9, 6
Organized list (ascending): 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 9, 9
💡 Tip: Organizing raw data into an ordered list is the very first step before making a tally table or a graph.

check.q: Tap to try: arrange this raw data in ascending order: 5, 3, 8, 3, 5, 5.
check.answer: Ascending order: 3, 3, 5, 5, 5, 8.

levels.miaWin: Wonderful! You can now turn messy raw data into a neat, organized list! 🚀

levels.title: Making Tally Marks
levels.mia: Tally marks are a super-fast way to count as data comes in, one item at a time — and every 5th mark makes a special group!
levels.body:
A tally mark is a single small line (|) drawn for each item counted. After 4 marks, the 5th mark is drawn diagonally across the first four, making an easy-to-count bundle of 5.

💡 Tip: Draw the diagonal 5th line firmly across the group — it makes each bundle of 5 instantly recognisable at a glance.

check.q: Tap to try: how many tally marks would you draw to show the count 9?
check.answer: One bundle of 5 (||||̸) plus 4 more single lines (||||) = 9.

levels.miaWin: Yes! You can now make tally marks like a pro counter! 🎉

levels.title: Counting Frequency from Tally Marks
levels.mia: Now let's go the OTHER way — reading a group of tally marks and quickly finding the total count, called the FREQUENCY!
levels.body:
The frequency of an item is how many times it occurs. To read tally marks fast: count the number of complete bundles of 5, multiply by 5, then add any leftover single marks.

Example: Tally marks show 2 full bundles of 5 plus 3 single marks. Frequency = (2 × 5) + 3 = 13.
💡 Tip: Counting in bundles of 5 is much faster and less error-prone than counting every single tally line one by one.

check.q: Tap to try: tally marks show 3 full bundles of 5 plus 1 single mark. What is the frequency?

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You can now read any tally chart in seconds! 🚀

levels.title: Building a Frequency Table
levels.mia: A frequency table is where tally marks and counts come together in one neat, organized chart — let's build one!
levels.body:
A frequency table lists each item (or category) alongside its tally marks and its frequency (the final count). It turns messy raw data into something instantly readable.

💡 Tip: Always add a 'Frequency' column with the final number — it saves you from re-counting tally marks every time you read the table.

check.q: Tap to try: in the fruit table above, which fruit was chosen the MOST?
check.answer: Mango — it has the highest frequency, 6.

levels.miaWin: Yes! You've built and understood your first frequency table! 🎉

levels.title: Reading & Using Frequency Tables
levels.mia: Now let's put a frequency table to work — answering real questions just by reading it carefully!
levels.body:
Once data is organized in a frequency table, you can quickly answer questions like: which category has the most/least, what is the total, or how many chose a specific option.

Example: A table shows: Cricket–12, Football–8, Badminton–5. Total students surveyed = 12+8+5 = 25. Cricket is the most popular; Badminton is the least popular.
💡 Tip: To find the TOTAL number of items in a frequency table, simply add up every frequency in the table.

check.q: Tap to try: a table shows Red–7, Blue–10, Green–4. What is the total number of people surveyed?

levels.miaWin: Brilliant! You can now read and use any frequency table with confidence! 🚀

levels.title: What is a Pictograph?
levels.mia: A pictograph tells a data story using PICTURES instead of plain numbers — let's see how a picture can equal a whole group!
levels.body:
A pictograph represents data using small pictures or symbols. Each picture stands for a fixed number of items, shown in a key (for example, 🍎 = 2 apples sold).

💡 Tip: ALWAYS check the key first before reading a pictograph — one picture might stand for 1, 2, 5, or even 10 items!

check.q: Tap to try: if the key says 🍦 = 2, and Wednesday shows 4 pictures, how many ice-creams were sold on Wednesday?
check.answer: 4 pictures × 2 ice-creams each = 8 ice-creams sold on Wednesday.

levels.miaWin: Yes! You've decoded your first pictograph! 🎉

levels.title: Drawing a Pictograph with a Key
levels.mia: Now let's flip it around — turning a frequency table INTO a pictograph, picture by picture!
levels.body:
To draw a pictograph: choose a simple symbol, decide a sensible key value (like 1 symbol = 5 units), then draw the right number of symbols for each category — using half-symbols for leftover amounts.

Example: If 15 students like Cricket and the key is ⚽ = 5 students, draw exactly 3 footballs (⚽⚽⚽) for Cricket. If 12 students like Football, draw 2 full footballs plus 1 half football (⚽⚽◐) for the extra 2 students.
💡 Tip: Choose a key value that divides your numbers EVENLY where possible — it avoids messy half-symbols and makes the pictograph easier to read.

check.q: Tap to try: if the key is 📕 = 10 books, how many symbols would you draw for 30 books?

levels.miaWin: Wonderful! You can now design your own pictograph from scratch! 🚀

levels.title: Reading Values from a Pictograph
levels.mia: Reading a pictograph is like solving a fun little puzzle — count the symbols, then multiply by the key!
levels.body:
To find the value for any row: count the number of symbols for that row, then multiply by the key value. Half-symbols count as half the key value.

💡 Tip: Always multiply the SYMBOL COUNT by the KEY VALUE — never just count the symbols as the final answer!

check.q: Tap to try: using the pictograph above, how many books did Kabir read?
check.answer: Kabir has 5 symbols × 2 books each = 10 books.

levels.miaWin: Yes! You're now reading pictographs like a data detective! 🎉

levels.title: Answering Questions Using a Pictograph
levels.mia: Let's use a pictograph to answer real comparison questions — who read the most, and by how many books!
levels.body:
Pictographs are great for quickly comparing categories — spot which row has the MOST or FEWEST symbols, then calculate exact values to find differences.

Example: Using the Books Read pictograph (key 📗 = 2): Aarav = 4×2 = 8, Riya = 2×2 = 4, Kabir = 5×2 = 10. Kabir read the most. Kabir read 10 − 4 = 6 more books than Riya.
💡 Tip: For 'how many more/fewer' questions, first calculate the actual values for both categories, THEN subtract.

check.q: Tap to try: using the same pictograph, how many more books did Aarav read than Riya?
check.answer: Aarav = 8 books, Riya = 4 books. 8 − 4 = 4 more books.

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You can now answer any pictograph question with confidence! 🚀

levels.title: What is a Bar Graph?
levels.mia: A bar graph tells a data story using tall bars instead of pictures — the taller the bar, the bigger the number!
levels.body:
A bar graph uses rectangular bars to show values. The height (or length) of each bar represents the frequency, measured against a numbered scale on the axis.

💡 Tip: A bar's height is read against the scale on the side — always trace a line straight across from the bar's top to the scale to get an exact value.

check.q: Tap to try: in the graph above, which pet is the LEAST popular?
check.answer: Fish — its bar is the shortest, reaching only about 2 on the scale.

levels.miaWin: Yes! You've read your first bar graph! 🎉

levels.title: Drawing a Bar Graph
levels.mia: Now let's build a bar graph from scratch — choosing a scale, then drawing each bar to the exact right height!
levels.body:
To draw a bar graph: pick a suitable scale for the numbers (e.g. each square = 2 units), draw bars of equal width with equal gaps between them, and make each bar's height match its data value.

Example: If Cricket = 12 students and the scale is 1 square = 2 students, the Cricket bar should be drawn 6 squares tall (12 ÷ 2 = 6).
💡 Tip: Keep every bar the SAME width, with the SAME gap between bars — only the HEIGHT should change to show different values.

check.q: Tap to try: if the scale is 1 square = 5 students, how many squares tall should a bar for 20 students be?
check.answer: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 squares tall.

levels.miaWin: Brilliant! You can now draw a neat, accurate bar graph! 🚀

levels.title: Reading Values from a Bar Graph
levels.mia: Reading a bar graph precisely means tracing carefully from the top of each bar over to the scale!
levels.body:
To read a bar's exact value: find the top of the bar, trace a straight horizontal line across to the scale (y-axis), and read off the number.

💡 Tip: If a bar's top falls BETWEEN two scale marks, estimate its value as roughly halfway (or the correct fraction) between them.

check.q: Tap to try: in the graph above, roughly how many students prefer Science?
check.answer: About 27 students — the Science bar reaches close to the very top of the scale (30).

levels.miaWin: Yes! You're reading bar graphs with real precision now! 🎉

levels.title: Comparing Bars & Finding Differences
levels.mia: Bar graphs are perfect for spotting patterns FAST — let's compare bars and calculate exact differences!
levels.body:
To compare two bars: read the value of each bar, then subtract to find the difference. The tallest bar is always the maximum; the shortest is the minimum.

Example: If the Science bar = 28 and the English bar = 12, the difference is 28 − 12 = 16 more students prefer Science than English.
💡 Tip: Always double-check which bar is taller BEFORE subtracting — the bigger value always comes first to avoid a negative answer.

check.q: Tap to try: if the Maths bar = 18 and the English bar = 12, how many more students prefer Maths than English?
check.answer: 18 − 12 = 6 more students prefer Maths.

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You can now compare and calculate from any bar graph! 🚀

levels.title: Comparing Data Across Tables & Graphs
levels.mia: Data handling isn't just about reading ONE chart — it's about comparing data across tables, pictographs, AND bar graphs together!
levels.body:
The same data can be shown as a frequency table, a pictograph, or a bar graph — they all carry the same information in different visual forms. Being able to compare across all three is a key skill.

💡 Tip: Whichever form data is shown in, always start by identifying what each category and each unit stands for before comparing.

check.q: Tap to think: if a bar graph and a pictograph both show the SAME survey results, will the values match?
check.answer: Yes! The underlying data is identical — only the visual style (bars vs pictures) is different.

levels.miaWin: Yes! You now understand how different data displays connect! 🎉

levels.title: Finding Maximum, Minimum & Totals
levels.mia: Whatever the chart, three questions come up again and again: what's the MOST, the LEAST, and the TOTAL. Let's master all three!
levels.body:
In any table or graph: the maximum is the highest value (tallest bar/most symbols/highest frequency), the minimum is the lowest, and the total is the sum of ALL values added together.

Example: A table shows Cricket–15, Football–9, Kabaddi–6. Maximum: Cricket (15). Minimum: Kabaddi (6). Total: 15+9+6 = 30 students surveyed.
💡 Tip: To find the total, add every single value in the table or graph — don't just look at the biggest bar!

check.q: Tap to try: a table shows Red–8, Blue–5, Yellow–11. What is the maximum, minimum, and total?
check.answer: Maximum: Yellow (11). Minimum: Blue (5). Total: 8+5+11 = 24.

levels.miaWin: Brilliant! You can now find the max, min, and total in any data set! 🚀

levels.title: Solving Data Word Problems — Tables & Tally
levels.mia: Let's put tally marks and frequency tables to work solving real word problems, step by step!
levels.body:
For table and tally word problems: first identify what's being asked (a single value, a total, or a comparison), then read the exact numbers carefully from the table before calculating.

Example: A survey shows tally marks for favourite subjects: Maths (||||̄ ||||̄ |), Science (||||̄ ||). Maths = 11, Science = 7. How many more students chose Maths? 11 − 7 = 4 more students.
💡 Tip: Convert ALL tally marks to numbers FIRST, then do any addition, subtraction, or comparison needed by the question.

check.q: Tap to try: a tally shows Tea (||||̄ |||) and Coffee (||||̄). How many people were surveyed in total?
check.answer: Tea = 8, Coffee = 5. Total = 8 + 5 = 13 people.

levels.miaWin: Yes! You're solving data word problems with real confidence! 🎉

levels.title: Solving Data Word Problems — Graphs
levels.mia: Now let's tackle word problems based on pictographs and bar graphs — reading carefully is the key!
levels.body:
For graph-based word problems: read each bar or symbol value accurately first (don't estimate!), then perform the addition, subtraction, or comparison the question asks for.

Example: A bar graph shows books sold: Monday = 20, Tuesday = 35, Wednesday = 15. Total books sold over the 3 days = 20+35+15 = 70. Tuesday sold 35−15 = 20 more books than Wednesday.
💡 Tip: Break multi-part graph word problems into small steps — find each individual value first, then combine them for the final answer.

check.q: Tap to try: a pictograph (key 🚗 = 4 cars) shows Red cars = 3 symbols, Blue cars = 2 symbols. How many more red cars are there than blue cars?
check.answer: Red = 3×4 = 12, Blue = 2×4 = 8. Difference = 12 − 8 = 4 more red cars.

levels.miaWin: Incredible! You've completed the entire Data Handling chapter — tables, pictographs, bar graphs, and word problems mastered! 🏅

levels.title: Quick-Fire Fill in the Blanks
levels.mia: Let's do a rapid recap of everything you've learned in Data Handling — fill in each blank in your head before checking!
levels.body:
Try these quick recap questions. Think of your answer first, then reveal it below to check yourself.

1. A collection of facts and figures gathered for a purpose is called ______.
Answer: data
2. The 5th tally mark is drawn ______ across the first four.
Answer: diagonally
3. In a frequency table, the final count for each item is called its ______.
Answer: frequency
4. In a pictograph, the box that tells you what each symbol is worth is called the ______.
Answer: key
5. In a bar graph, the ______ of each bar shows its value.
Answer: height (or length)
💡 Tip: Cover the answer with your hand, say your guess out loud, THEN check — it helps the learning stick much better!

check.q: Tap to try one more: the highest value in a data set is called the ______.
check.answer: maximum

levels.miaWin: Awesome recap! Your Data Handling fill-in-the-blank skills are sharp! ⭐

levels.title: True or False Challenge
levels.mia: Now let's test your instincts — is each Data Handling statement TRUE or FALSE? Think fast!
levels.body:
Read each statement, decide TRUE or FALSE, then check your answer.

1. Raw data is data that has already been organized into a table.
Answer: FALSE — raw data is data exactly as collected, before organizing.
2. Every symbol in a pictograph must always represent exactly 1 item.
Answer: FALSE — a symbol can represent any fixed number, shown in the key (1, 2, 5, 10, etc.).
3. In a bar graph, all bars should have the same width.
Answer: TRUE — only the height changes to represent different values.
4. The total of a frequency table is found by adding up every frequency.
Answer: TRUE — summing all frequencies gives the overall total.
5. A tally mark bundle always groups items in sets of 10.
Answer: FALSE — tally marks are bundled in sets of 5, with the 5th mark drawn diagonally.
💡 Tip: When unsure, picture the actual chart or table in your mind — it often makes the true/false answer obvious.

check.q: Tap to try: TRUE or FALSE — a pictograph and a bar graph can represent the exact same underlying data.
check.answer: TRUE — they are just two different visual styles for showing the same information.

levels.miaWin: Fantastic! You've completed the full Data Handling practice round-up — great work! 🏅
